title: Linear-size labeled sample compression
open: Does every binary concept class of VC dimension \(d\) admit a labeled sample-compression scheme of size linear in \(d\), independent of the original sample size? Formally, is there a constant \(c\) such that every class of VC dimension \(d\) has a compression scheme of size \(c \cdot d\)?
status: The problem originates with Littlestone and Warmuth in 1986. General schemes of size exponential in \(d\) are known, but the linear bound remains open. Key works include Littlestone and Warmuth (1986), *Relating Data Compression and Learnability*; Moran and Yehudayoff (2016), *Sample Compression Schemes for VC Classes*, arXiv:1503.06960; and Attias et al. (2025), *Sample Compression Scheme Reductions*, arXiv:2410.13012.
solved_when: A construction (or proof of existence) of a labeled sample-compression scheme of size \(O(d)\) for every binary concept class of VC dimension \(d\), with no dependence on the sample size; alternatively, a counterexample class exhibiting superlinear necessary size.
why: It would give a universal explanation of learnability through small reconstructible certificates, tying generalization directly to compression.
key_works: Littlestone and Warmuth (1986), *Relating Data Compression and Learnability*; Moran and Yehudayoff (2016), *Sample Compression Schemes for VC Classes*, arXiv:1503.06960; Attias et al. (2025), *Sample Compression Scheme Reductions*, arXiv:2410.13012.

title: Linear-size unlabeled compression
open: Does every binary concept class of VC dimension \(d\) admit an unlabeled compression scheme whose size is linear in \(d\), so that a concept can be recovered from a subset of the sample without storing the labels of the selected examples?
status: The stronger conjecture that size exactly \(d\) always suffices is false: Pálvölgyi and Tardos constructed counterexamples (arXiv:1811.12471), but these do not settle whether a universal linear bound holds. Kuzmin and Warmuth (2007) established unlabeled compression schemes of size \(d\) for maximum classes.
solved_when: A proof that every binary VC class has an unlabeled compression scheme of size \(O(d)\), or a counterexample class for which no such linear-size scheme exists.
why: It would cleanly separate the information conveyed by which examples are selected from the information explicitly carried by their labels, clarifying the minimal information needed to encode a learned concept.
key_works: Kuzmin and Warmuth (2007), *Unlabeled Compression Schemes for Maximum Classes*; Pálvölgyi and Tardos (2021 version), *Unlabeled Compression Schemes Exceeding the VC-dimension*, arXiv:1811.12471.

title: Polynomial exact compression for agnostic absolute-loss regression
open: Does every real-valued function class of finite pseudo-dimension admit an exact agnostic compression scheme whose size is polynomial in that dimension, under absolute loss?
status: Explicitly posed in 2024 by Attias, Hanneke, Kontorovich, and Sadigurschi (*Agnostic Sample Compression Schemes for Regression*, PMLR 235:2069–2085). Bounded approximate schemes are available, but the general exact polynomial-size statement remains a separate question.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) is given for the general statement: every class of finite pseudo-dimension d has an exact agnostic compression scheme of size polynomial in d under absolute loss.
why: It would turn noisy regression solutions into small, loss-preserving training certificates.
key_works: Attias, Hanneke, Kontorovich, and Sadigurschi (2024), *Agnostic Sample Compression Schemes for Regression*, PMLR 235:2069–2085.

title: Polynomial fat-dimension compression for squared-loss regression
open: Under squared loss, can approximate agnostic compression for regression always be achieved with size polynomial in the appropriate scale-dependent fat-shattering dimension and the accuracy parameters? More precisely, is there a construction whose compression size is polynomially bounded in the fat-shattering dimension at the relevant scale, rather than merely exponentially dependent on it?
status: This is an explicit 2024 question (Attias et al., 2024, *Agnostic Sample Compression Schemes for Regression*; Attias et al., 2025, *Sample Compression Scheme Reductions*, arXiv:2410.13012). Generic constructions have exponential dimension dependence, while linear regression admits substantially smaller schemes.
solved_when: A scheme is given whose compression size is polynomial in the scale-dependent fat-shattering dimension and the accuracy parameters, for approximate agnostic compression under squared loss.
why: It would connect real-valued learnability to practically useful dataset reduction, yielding compact coresets for regression rather than worst-case exponential blowups.
key_works: Attias et al. (2024), *Agnostic Sample Compression Schemes for Regression*; Attias et al. (2025), *Sample Compression Scheme Reductions*, arXiv:2410.13012.

title: Local regularization for all PAC-learnable multiclass classes
open: Can every PAC-learnable multiclass class be learned by selecting sample-consistent hypotheses via a regularizer that depends only on the hypothesis and the test point? In other words, does there exist, for every PAC-learnable multiclass hypothesis class, a local regularizer whose induced selection rule achieves PAC learnability?
status: Posed in 2024 by Asilis et al. in *Open Problem: Can Local Regularization Learn All Multiclass Problems?*. The analogous transductive statement was disproved in 2025 by Jafar, Asilis, and Dughmi in *Local Regularizers Are Not Transductive Learners* (arXiv:2502.07187), whose negative result explicitly leaves the PAC question open.
solved_when: A proof that, for every PAC-learnable multiclass hypothesis class, some regularizer of the form (hypothesis, test point) → value, applied to sample-consistent hypotheses, yields a PAC learner; or a counterexample class that is PAC-learnable but not learnable by any such local regularization scheme.
why: It tests whether regularization can remain a universal organizing principle for learning beyond binary classification, and it delineates the boundary between local (per-test-point) and global selection rules.
key_works: Asilis et al. (2024), *Open Problem: Can Local Regularization Learn All Multiclass Problems?*; Jafar, Asilis, and Dughmi (2025), *Local Regularizers Are Not Transductive Learners*, arXiv:2502.07187.

title: Exact list-length composition
open: How much prediction ambiguity compounds when learning a product class — must a learner output lists whose length multiplies the minimal list sizes of the factors, or can it do better? Formally, determine the minimum list size needed to learn a product class from the minimum list sizes of its factors, including characterizing when the known upper and lower composition bounds are attained.
status: The problem is posed explicitly in the 2024 direct-sums program (Hanneke, Moran, and Waknine, 2024, *Open Problem: Direct Sums in Learning Theory*; cf. Charikar and Pabbaraju, 2023, *A Characterization of List Learnability*). Known bounds involving products of the factor list sizes leave a nontrivial gap between the upper and lower composition regimes.
solved_when: An exact characterization of the minimal list size for product classes is given, matching the known upper and lower composition bounds — in particular, identifying when the product of the factor list sizes is necessary and when it is not.
why: It quantifies how prediction ambiguity compounds in structured outputs, determining whether ambiguity grows multiplicatively under composition or can be tamed.
key_works: Hanneke, Moran, and Waknine (2024), *Open Problem: Direct Sums in Learning Theory*; Charikar and Pabbaraju (2023), *A Characterization of List Learnability*.

title: Distribution-free DNF learning with membership queries
open: Is there a polynomial-time PAC learner for polynomial-size DNF formulas under arbitrary input distributions when the learner is additionally allowed membership queries? In other words, does active access to labels suffice to make distribution-free DNF learning computationally tractable?
status: A longstanding open problem. Recent locally mixing random-walk methods of Alman, Nadimpalli, Patel, and Servedio (2025), *DNF Learning via Locally Mixing Random Walks*, improve the algorithmic landscape but do not establish the general polynomial-time target.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm exists that PAC-learns the class of polynomial-size DNF formulas over arbitrary input distributions, given both random examples and membership queries; or a proof that no such polynomial-time learner exists under standard assumptions.
why: It isolates whether active access to labels overcomes the computational difficulty of distribution-free DNF learning, the canonical open barrier between query access and passive learning.
key_works: Alman, Nadimpalli, Patel, and Servedio (2025), *DNF Learning via Locally Mixing Random Walks*.

title: Fixed-parameter tractable learning of juntas
open: Can an arbitrary \(k\)-junta on \(n\) variables be learned from uniform random examples in time polynomial in \(n\), \(2^k\), and \(1/\epsilon\)? Formally, the goal is an algorithm with running time \(\operatorname{poly}(n,2^k,1/\epsilon)\) rather than \(n^{\Omega(k)}\)-type search.

solved_when: An algorithm learns any \(k\)-junta to accuracy \(\epsilon\) from uniform random examples in time \(\operatorname{poly}(n,2^k,1/\epsilon)\).
why: It would efficiently discover a small unknown relevant feature set without favorable signal assumptions.

title: Polynomial-time learning parity with noise
open: Can an unknown parity function on \(n\) bits be learned—or its values predicted—in polynomial time from uniformly random examples whose labels are flipped with independent constant-rate noise? Alternatively, prove that no such efficient learner exists under a standard complexity assumption.
status: Open for decades. Subexponential-time algorithms and numerous parameter-specific improvements are known; general polynomial-time learning remains unresolved and would undermine widely used LPN hardness assumptions. Key works: Blum, Kalai, and Wasserman (2003), *Noise-tolerant Learning, the Parity Problem, and the Statistical Query Model*; Golowich et al. (2024), *On Learning Parities with Dependent Noise*, arXiv:2404.11325.
solved_when: Either a polynomial-time algorithm for learning parity with constant noise rate from uniform examples is given, or a hardness result is established from a standard complexity assumption ruling out such an algorithm.
why: It is a basic test case for noisy-learning theory, and polynomial-time learning would undermine the LPN hardness assumptions underlying widely deployed lightweight cryptography.
key_works: Blum, Kalai, and Wasserman (2003), *Noise-tolerant Learning, the Parity Problem, and the Statistical Query Model*; Golowich et al. (2024), *On Learning Parities with Dependent Noise*, arXiv:2404.11325.

title: Mansour’s conjecture
open: Does every DNF formula of size \(s\) concentrate all but \(\epsilon\) of its Fourier mass on \(s^{O_\epsilon(1)}\) coefficients? The customary stronger formulation asks for \(s^{O(\log(1/\epsilon))}\).
status: The conjecture originates in Mansour's 1990s Fourier-concentration work. General quasi-polynomial concentration bounds are known, and stronger results hold for restricted or random DNFs: Klivans, Lee, and Wan (2010) proved Mansour's conjecture true for random DNF formulas, and Lecomte and Tan (2021) (*Sharper Bounds on the Fourier Concentration of DNFs*, arXiv:2109.04525) obtained sharper bounds.
solved_when: A proof that, for every size-\(s\) DNF, all but \(\epsilon\) of the Fourier mass is supported on \(s^{O_\epsilon(1)}\) coefficients — or, in the stronger form, on \(s^{O(\log(1/\epsilon))}\) coefficients.
why: It would yield efficient Fourier-based learning of DNF and explain the spectral simplicity of DNF formulas.
key_works: Mansour’s 1990s Fourier-concentration work; Klivans, Lee, and Wan (2010), *Mansour’s Conjecture Is True for Random DNF Formulas*; Lecomte and Tan (2021), *Sharper Bounds on the Fourier Concentration of DNFs*, arXiv:2109.04525.

title: Distribution-independent neural SGD versus linear learning
open: If a benign neural architecture can be learned by gradient descent or SGD under every input distribution, must an appropriately efficient linear-model learner also exist? More precisely: does distribution-independent learnability by standard SGD force the existence of a comparably efficient learner that is effectively linear?
status: This is an explicit 2026 question, posed by Feldman, Kamath, and Srebro (2026), *Is the Power of Deep Learning over Linear Models Inherently Distribution Dependent?*, and it is distinct from the statistical-query formulation because standard SGD need not behave like an arbitrary SQ algorithm — a point also examined by Barzilai and Shamir (2026), *Limitations of SGD for Multi-Index Models Beyond Statistical Queries*.
solved_when: A proof that whenever SGD learns such an architecture under every input distribution, an efficient linear-model learner exists; or a counterexample — a benign architecture learnable by SGD in a distribution-independent way with no efficient linear learner.
why: It would locate the source of deep learning's advantages in architecture, optimization, or distributional structure, rather than leaving the question conflated with statistical-query limitations.
key_works: Feldman, Kamath, and Srebro (2026), *Is the Power of Deep Learning over Linear Models Inherently Distribution Dependent?*; Barzilai and Shamir (2026), *Limitations of SGD for Multi-Index Models Beyond Statistical Queries*.

title: Planted clique below the square-root scale
open: Is there a randomized polynomial-time algorithm that detects or recovers a planted clique of size \(n^{1/2-\delta}\) in an Erdős–Rényi graph, for any fixed \(\delta>0\)? Or can such an algorithm be proved impossible under a standard assumption?
status: Open for decades. Strong lower bounds are known for restricted algorithmic families, including bounded-degree sum-of-squares (Barak et al., 2016, arXiv:1604.03084; Kunisky, Wein, and Bandeira, 2019, arXiv:1907.11636), but not for all polynomial-time algorithms.
solved_when: Either a randomized polynomial-time algorithm reliably detects or recovers planted cliques of size \(n^{1/2-\delta}\) for some fixed \(\delta>0\), or a lower bound is established against all polynomial-time algorithms under a standard assumption.
why: Planted-clique hardness underpins many proposed computational barriers in statistics and learning, so resolving it either way would firm up or overturn a large body of evidence-based conjecture.
key_works: Barak et al. (2016), *A Nearly Tight Sum-of-Squares Lower Bound for the Planted Clique Problem*, arXiv:1604.03084; Kunisky, Wein, and Bandeira (2019), *Notes on Computational Hardness of Hypothesis Testing*, arXiv:1907.11636.

title: Sharp polynomial-time sparse-PCA phase diagram
open: Does the sparse spiked covariance model admit a sharp statistical–computational phase diagram — that is, can we characterize exactly when detection and recovery of a sparse spike are possible in polynomial time? Formally, determine the exact computational thresholds across sparsity, dimension, sample size, and signal strength.
status: Conditional reductions and restricted-model lower bounds (e.g., Berthet and Rigollet, 2013, arXiv:1304.0828; Kunisky et al., 2019, arXiv:1907.11636) establish substantial statistical–computational gaps, but a complete algorithmic phase diagram is not established.
solved_when: The polynomial-time detection and recovery thresholds for the sparse spiked covariance model are pinned down exactly in terms of sparsity, dimension, sample size, and signal strength, with matching algorithms and lower bounds.
why: It would tell us whether a failure to find sparse latent factors reflects insufficient data or insufficient computation — a distinction that currently cannot be made sharply.
key_works: Berthet and Rigollet (2013), *Computational Lower Bounds for Sparse PCA*, arXiv:1304.0828; Kunisky et al. (2019), *Notes on Computational Hardness of Hypothesis Testing*, arXiv:1907.11636.

title: Computational threshold for spiked tensor recovery
open: Can a polynomial-time algorithm recover a rank-one signal planted in Gaussian tensor noise at signal strengths well below the best known spectral and iterative thresholds, or does a genuine computational barrier hold there? Formally, is there an efficient estimator succeeding in the regime between the information-theoretic threshold and the currently established algorithmic thresholds for spiked tensor recovery?
status: The statistical–computational separation has been investigated since 2014, beginning with Montanari and Richard (2014), *A Statistical Model for Tensor PCA* (arXiv:1411.1076). Information-theoretic thresholds are well characterized — notably via Jagannath and collaborators (2020), *Statistical Thresholds for Tensor PCA*, DOI:10.1214/19-AAP1547 — and the limitations of several specific algorithmic families are understood, but the power of unrestricted polynomial-time computation remains open.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm is proved to recover the rank-one spike at signal strengths substantially below the known spectral and iterative thresholds, or a proof (e.g., via a restricted class of algorithms or reductions) shows no polynomial-time algorithm succeeds in that regime.
why: It would settle whether the observed statistical–computational gap for tensor PCA is real or an artifact of our algorithmic toolkit, with direct consequences for latent-variable estimation, higher-order statistics, and learning nonlinear features.
key_works: Montanari and Richard (2014), *A Statistical Model for Tensor PCA*, arXiv:1411.1076; Jagannath and collaborators (2020), *Statistical Thresholds for Tensor PCA*, DOI:10.1214/19-AAP1547.

title: Constant-factor instance-optimal identity testing
open: Is there a concise functional \(\Phi(q,\epsilon)\) that characterizes, up to universal constant factors, the number of samples needed to distinguish \(p=q\) from \(\mathrm{TV}(p,q)>\epsilon\)? In other words, can the instance-optimal sample complexity of identity testing be captured within constant factors by a single explicit functional of the reference distribution \(q\) and the error parameter \(\epsilon\)?
status: An explicit COLT 2024 problem. Existing characterizations involve differently truncated norms whose bounds need not agree within constant factors. Key works: Valiant and Valiant (2014), *An Automatic Inequality Prover and Instance Optimal Identity Testing*; Canonne (2024), *Open Problem: Tight Characterization of Instance-Optimal Identity Testing*.
solved_when: An explicit functional \(\Phi(q,\epsilon)\) is given, together with matching upper and lower bounds on the sample complexity of testing \(p=q\) versus \(\mathrm{TV}(p,q)>\epsilon\) that agree within universal constant factors.
why: A solution would tell an experimenter how difficult a specific goodness-of-fit problem actually is, replacing competing characterizations with a single usable yardstick.
key_works: Valiant and Valiant (2014), *An Automatic Inequality Prover and Instance Optimal Identity Testing*; Canonne (2024), *Open Problem: Tight Characterization of Instance-Optimal Identity Testing*.

title: Adaptive conditional-independence testing under unknown smoothness
open: When the smoothness of the underlying functions and the effective dimension of the conditioning variable are both unknown, how much harder does nonparametric conditional-independence testing become compared to the case where these parameters are known? Formally, under an explicit nonparametric smoothness model, determine the unavoidable adaptation penalty for conditional-independence testing when smoothness and effective conditioning dimension must be learned from data.
status: Research target. Unrestricted distribution-free conditional-independence testing is already impossible (Shah and Peters, 2020, *The Hardness of Conditional Independence Testing and the Generalised Covariance Measure*, arXiv:1804.07203), so the question concerns restricted, testable model families; no results yet exist for the adaptive setting.
solved_when: Sharp (minimax-rate) characterisation of the adaptation penalty is established — i.e., matching upper and lower bounds for the testing rate under unknown smoothness and unknown effective conditioning dimension relative to the rate achievable when both are known, within the stated nonparametric smoothness model.
why: Causal discovery and graphical-model procedures rely on conditional-independence tests whose assumed regularity parameters are rarely known in practice; quantifying the adaptation penalty tells us when reliable, assumption-light edge removal is actually possible.
key_works: Shah and Peters (2020), *The Hardness of Conditional Independence Testing and the Generalised Covariance Measure*, arXiv:1804.07203.

title: Robust regression beyond SQ sample barriers
open: Can unrestricted polynomial-time algorithms for robust regression achieve error below the barriers established for statistical-query algorithms using subquadratic samples, or can those barriers be extended to broader computational models? solved_when: Either a polynomial-time algorithm (outside the SQ class) achieves error below the \(O(\sqrt{\epsilon\kappa})\) barrier with subquadratic samples, or the barrier is proven as an impossibility for general polynomial-time computation.
why: It determines whether the known limits reflect weaknesses of current proof models or genuine limits of robust statistics itself, directly shaping which algorithmic approaches are worth pursuing.

title: Black-box reductions to adaptive nonconvex optimization
open: Can optimal online convex algorithms be converted, by a purely black-box reduction, into stochastic optimizers for nonconvex objectives that retain meaningful adaptive guarantees? solved_when: An explicit black-box reduction exists that takes any optimal online convex algorithm and yields a stochastic nonconvex optimizer whose adaptive guarantees are preserved in a meaningful sense — in particular, going beyond a worst-case stationary-point rate.
why: It would let progress in online learning be immediately reused in practical adaptive optimization, rather than requiring adaptive methods to be redesigned from scratch for nonconvex settings.

title: Sharp stochastic tradeoffs for stepsize-only acceleration
open: What is the best tradeoff between bias decay and noise amplification that plain SGD — no momentum, only a predetermined sequence of varying stepsizes — can achieve under stochastic gradients? Equivalently, characterize the optimal simultaneous rates of bias decay and noise amplification achievable by stepsize-only acceleration.
status: Research target. Deterministic stepsize hedging is now well understood at the exponent level (Altschuler and Parrilo, 2025, *Acceleration by Stepsize Hedging I*, arXiv:2309.07879; cf. Chen and Hazan, 2024), but its full finite-sample stochastic frontier remains a separate open problem.
solved_when: A sharp characterization of the achievable frontier between bias decay and noise amplification for SGD with predetermined varying stepsizes and no momentum, with matching upper and lower bounds.
why: A deterministic speedup is useful for learning only if stochastic gradients do not erase it; without this characterization, stepsize-only acceleration offers no guaranteed stochastic benefit.
key_works: Altschuler and Parrilo (2025), *Acceleration by Stepsize Hedging I*, arXiv:2309.07879; Chen and Hazan (2024), *Black-Box Reductions and Adaptive Gradient Methods for Nonconvex Optimization*.

title: Sharp algorithm-dependent generalization beyond interpolation
open: Can we give an efficiently computable generalization bound that treats the same network differently depending on how it was trained — separating the case where it interpolates meaningful labels from the case where it interpolates randomly assigned labels, and predicting the resulting gap in population risk?
status: The target is motivated by experiments since 2017. Capacity-only explanations, and several forms of uniform convergence, are known to be insufficient in existing constructions; see Zhang et al. (2017), *Understanding Deep Learning Requires Rethinking Generalization*, arXiv:1611.03530, and Nagarajan and Kolter (2019), *Uniform Convergence May Be Unable to Explain Generalization in Deep Learning*, arXiv:1902.04742.
solved_when: Such a bound exists, is efficiently evaluable, distinguishes identical architectures trained to interpolate meaningful versus random labels, and quantitatively predicts their population-risk difference.
why: It isolates what the training algorithm and data structure contribute to generalization beyond parameter count, where capacity-only measures provably fail.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2017), *Understanding Deep Learning Requires Rethinking Generalization*, arXiv:1611.03530; Nagarajan and Kolter (2019), *Uniform Convergence May Be Unable to Explain Generalization in Deep Learning*, arXiv:1902.04742.

title: Near-observed-risk PAC-Bayes certificates at modern scale
open: Can we produce a generalization certificate for a large trained model that comes within a small prespecified gap — say two percentage points — of the model's observed risk, with the certificate chosen without access to the evaluation labels? Formally, the challenge is a preregistered PAC-Bayes bound whose value is near-observed-risk at modern model scale.
status: The target is proposed but unmet. Nonvacuous deep-network PAC-Bayes bounds already exist, e.g. Dziugaite and Roy (2017), *Computing Nonvacuous Generalization Bounds for Deep Stochastic Neural Networks* (arXiv:1703.11008); what remains open is achieving such bounds with sharpness, scale, and clean selection accounting.
solved_when: A preregistered generalization certificate is computed for a large trained model whose value lies within two percentage points of the observed risk, and the certificate's selection makes no use of the evaluation labels.
why: It would turn theoretical generalization bounds into usable evidence accompanying a model release, rather than numerically vacuous statements.
key_works: Dziugaite and Roy (2017), *Computing Nonvacuous Generalization Bounds for Deep Stochastic Neural Networks*, arXiv:1703.11008.

title: Necessary and sufficient conditions for nonlinear benign overfitting
open: When can a nonlinear predictor that learns its own features and perfectly interpolates noisy training labels still generalize well? Identify necessary and sufficient conditions under which such an interpolating, feature-learning nonlinear predictor achieves vanishing excess risk despite label noise.
status: For linear models, benign overfitting has precise spectral characterizations (Bartlett, Long, Lugosi, and Tsigser (2020), *Benign Overfitting in Linear Regression*, arXiv:1906.11300). An equally sharp theory covering learned nonlinear features, e.g. as arising in feature-learning networks (Yang and Hu (2021), *Feature Learning in Infinite-Width Neural Networks*, arXiv:2011.14522), remains a research frontier.
solved_when: A sharp characterization — analogous in precision to the spectral characterizations available for linear models — gives necessary and sufficient conditions for vanishing excess risk of an interpolating, feature-learning nonlinear predictor in the presence of label noise.
why: It would explain when fitting noise is harmless and when interpolation is dangerous, extending benign-overfitting theory to the regimes where modern neural networks actually operate.

title: Generalization through learned-feature transitions
open: When does a wide network stop behaving like its kernel limit and start genuinely learning features, and what is its risk throughout that transition? Concretely, in a specified teacher–student model, derive finite-width risk bounds that remain informative as training moves from kernel-like behavior to substantial feature learning.
status: Kernel-limit theory (Jacot, Gabriel, and Hongler, 2018, *Neural Tangent Kernel*, arXiv:1806.07572) and feature-learning-limit theory (Yang and Hu, 2021, *Feature Learning in Infinite-Width Neural Networks*, arXiv:2011.14522) both exist, but neither limit alone supplies a sharp finite-size bridge between their predictive regimes.
solved_when: A finite-width risk bound is derived for the teacher–student model that stays informative across the full transition from the kernel-like regime to the feature-learning regime, rather than degrading in either limit.
why: It would explain when adding width improves a model and when it suppresses useful representation learning.
key_works: Jacot, Gabriel, and Hongler (2018), *Neural Tangent Kernel*, arXiv:1806.07572; Yang and Hu (2021), *Feature Learning in Infinite-Width Neural Networks*, arXiv:2011.14522.

title: Quantifying useful versus incidental memorization
open: Can memorization in overparameterized models be split into a useful part — information the model genuinely needs for population performance — and an incidental part that can be removed without appreciably increasing risk? Formally, the goal is to define and estimate such a decomposition of what a fitted model retains from its training set.
status: This is currently a research target rather than an established result. Interpolation and memorization are empirically established (Zhang et al., 2017, *Understanding Deep Learning Requires Rethinking Generalization*, arXiv:1611.03530), but the mere fact that models fit individual examples is not yet a quantitative account of those examples' causal contribution to performance; related work on forgetting (Sekhari et al., 2021, *Remember What You Want to Forget*, arXiv:2103.03279) touches adjacent questions. Connections exist to minimal sufficient statistics in information theory and to causal inference on the effects of deleting training information.
solved_when: A decomposition of memorization into population-necessary information versus removable information is both defined and estimable in practice, with the removable component shown to incur no appreciable increase in (population) risk when deleted.
why: A quantitative account would directly inform compression, privacy, data valuation, and machine unlearning, replacing the current qualitative observation that interpolating models memorize.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2017), *Understanding Deep Learning Requires Rethinking Generalization*, arXiv:1611.03530; Sekhari et al. (2021), *Remember What You Want to Forget*, arXiv:2103.03279.

why: Different stationary margin solutions can generalize very differently.

title: Uniformly reliable hyperparameter transfer

open: Can we prove that a learning rate tuned on a small network will work on a much larger one, at realistic finite width and depth? solved_when: A general guarantee is proved that carries learning rates and related hyperparameters from a small model to a substantially larger one, with a useful bound on the finite-size error and handling of joint depth scaling.
why: It would let practitioners tune at small scale and deploy at large scale, removing much of the expensive hyperparameter search currently performed at full scale.

title: U-calibration for genuinely multidimensional outcomes
open: Can we extend U-calibration to outcomes that are multiclass or vector-valued, achieving regret guarantees that adapt simultaneously to every proper loss in a useful family? In other words, is there a forecasting algorithm whose predictions over the probability simplex are calibrated in a sense that yields optimal regret against the whole family of proper losses at once?
status: This is a research target extending binary forecasting results; the geometry and boundary behavior of multidimensional probability predictions create additional obstacles. Related work includes Frongillo et al. (2026), *Toward Simultaneously Optimal Regret in U-Calibration*, and Gibbs and Tibshirani (2026), *Sample-Efficient Omniprediction for Proper Losses*.
solved_when: A forecasting algorithm for multiclass or vector-valued outcomes is given with sharp simultaneously adaptive regret guarantees for a useful family of proper losses, together with matching analysis; no quantitative budgets are specified beyond the regret guarantee itself.
why: Most deployed forecasting systems predict more than a single binary event, so a multidimensional theory of U-calibration is needed for omniprediction guarantees to apply in practice.
key_works: Frongillo et al. (2026), *Toward Simultaneously Optimal Regret in U-Calibration*; Gibbs and Tibshirani (2026), *Sample-Efficient Omniprediction for Proper Losses*.

title: Heavy-tailed bandits with unknown moment parameters
open: What is the true price of adaptation in heavy-tailed bandits when the order of the finite moment and its bound are not known in advance — and, if full adaptation is impossible or costly, what is the weakest additional assumption under which near-oracle regret is achievable?
status: This is an explicit open problem posed at COLT 2025 by Genalti and Metta (correct per record: Genalti and Mettelli, 2025), *Open Problem: Regret Minimization in Heavy-Tailed Bandits with Unknown Distributional Parameters*. Most existing guarantees assume the moment parameters are known, and adaptation without restrictions cannot simply be presumed free.
solved_when: The optimal regret cost of adapting to both the moment order and the moment bound is characterized (matching upper and lower bounds), or a minimal assumption is identified under which regret matches the known-parameter oracle up to constants or lower-order terms.
why: Real reward distributions rarely arrive with certified tail parameters, so guarantees that presuppose them are of limited practical use.

title: Joint differential privacy in linear contextual bandits
open: What is the exact privacy price of personalization in linear contextual bandits — how much additional regret must an algorithm incur to guarantee joint differential privacy? why: It settles whether sequential personalization can protect each user's privacy without a prohibitive loss in learning performance, a question with direct bearing on privacy-preserving recommendation systems.

title: Tight discrete-time adaptive RKHS confidence bounds
open: How tight can confidence intervals for kernel (RKHS) regression be when the covariates are chosen adaptively, rather than i.i.d.? In particular, characterize when the standard information-gain or effective-dimension factors in the radii can be reduced while remaining valid under adaptive sampling.
status: Posed in 2021 (Vakili, Scarlett, and Javidi, 2021, *Open Problem: Tight Online Confidence Intervals for RKHS Elements*). A 2023 lower bound of Lattimore (*A Lower Bound for Linear and Kernel Regression with Adaptive Covariates*) rules out certain improvements in a continuous-time formulation; remaining discrete-time and structured-kernel refinements must respect that barrier.
solved_when: Sharp confidence radii for discrete-time kernel regression with adaptively chosen covariates are established, together with a specification of exactly when information-gain or dimension factors can be reduced (and matching lower bounds showing no further reduction is possible).
why: The width of these confidence intervals directly governs exploration efficiency in kernel bandits and control, so tighter radii translate into faster, more sample-efficient algorithms.
key_works: Vakili, Scarlett, and Javidi (2021), *Open Problem: Tight Online Confidence Intervals for RKHS Elements*; Lattimore (2023), *A Lower Bound for Linear and Kernel Regression with Adaptive Covariates*.

title: Instance-optimal equilibrium identification in matrix games
open: How many samples from a noisy two-player zero-sum matrix game are actually needed to identify its Nash equilibrium? The goal is a full instance-dependent characterization — capturing both payoff gaps and equilibrium geometry — with algorithms and matching lower bounds.
status: Posed as an explicit open problem at COLT 2025 by Maiti (2025), *Open Problem: Optimal Instance-Dependent Sample Complexity for Finding Nash Equilibrium in Two Player Zero-S-Sum Matrix Games*. Worst-case rates are known not to capture the full dependence on payoff gaps and equilibrium geometry; no instance-optimal characterization is known.
solved_when: A sample-complexity characterization, depending on the payoff gaps and the geometry of the equilibrium, is established with matching upper and lower bounds for identifying a Nash equilibrium of a noisy two-player zero-sum matrix game.
why: It extends best-arm identification from single decisions to competitive decisions with mixed strategies, where the hardness of the problem is shaped by the equilibrium itself, not just payoff gaps.
key_works: Maiti (2025), *Open Problem: Optimal Instance-Dependent Sample Complexity for Finding Nash Equilibrium in Two Player Zero-Sum Matrix Games*.

title: When SGD learns an in-context algorithm
open: Can we prove that standard training of a transformer by SGD actually learns an algorithm, not merely a predictor? Formally: for a specified distribution over regression or classification tasks, show that ordinary transformer training learns an in-context algorithm achieving near-optimal finite-sample risk.
status: It is known that transformers can represent useful statistical procedures, and experiments demonstrate in-context learning behavior; however, representation results and training-success guarantees remain distinct, and no theorem currently bridges them. Key works: Garg et al. (2022), *What Can Transformers Learn In-Context?*, arXiv:2208.01066; Bai et al. (2023), *Transformers as Statisticians*, arXiv:2306.04637.
solved_when: A theorem exists showing that, for an explicitly specified task distribution (regression or classification), transformer training via ordinary SGD yields an in-context algorithm whose finite-sample risk is near-optimal.
why: It would explain why pretraining produces learning algorithms rather than only flexible predictors, closing the gap between what transformers can represent and what training actually achieves.
key_works: Garg et al. (2022), *What Can Transformers Learn In-Context?*, arXiv:2208.01066; Bai et al. (2023), *Transformers as Statisticians*, arXiv:2306.04637.

title: Compositional error control for learned reasoning procedures
open: Can we prove end-to-end error guarantees for reasoning procedures built by composing learned subprocedures adaptively, when the subprocedures' mistakes may be correlated rather than independent across steps?
status: Guarantees currently exist only for isolated in-context estimators, e.g. Bai et al. (2023), *Transformers as Statisticians*, arXiv:2306.04637, and Foster, Block, and Misra (2024), *Is Behavior Cloning All You Need?*, arXiv:2407.15007; these do not automatically survive adaptive multi-step composition. Related ideas appear in reliability theory (dependent component failures) and control theory (closed-loop error amplification).
solved_when: A theoretical framework exists giving end-to-end error bounds for adaptively composed learned estimators under correlated per-step errors, covering long multi-step chains rather than isolated single-step in-context procedures.
why: A small local error can compound into a large failure probability over long reasoning chains, so without such guarantees the reliability of learned multi-step reasoning cannot be certified.
key_works: Bai et al. (2023), *Transformers as Statisticians*, arXiv:2306.04637; Foster, Block, and Misra (2024), *Is Behavior Cloning All You Need?*, arXiv:2407.15007.

title: Deriving language-model scaling exponents
subfield: Scaling laws, grokking, and mechanistic explanations
open: Can the power-law exponents governing language-model loss be derived from explicit assumptions about data structure, architecture, and optimization, rather than fitted after training? In other words, is there a first-principles account that predicts the scaling exponents before any training runs?
status: Empirical power laws have been documented since 2020, notably in Kaplan et al. (2020), *Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models* (arXiv:2001.08361) and Hoffmann et al. (2022), *Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models* (arXiv:2203.15556), but a broadly predictive first-principles account remains a research target.
solved_when: A theory yields predictive loss-scaling exponents that agree with the empirically observed power laws across data, model size, and compute, derived from stated assumptions rather than post-hoc fitting.
why: It would make scaling forecasts falsifiable outside the range used to fit them.
key_works: Kaplan et al. (2020), *Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models*, arXiv:2001.08361; Hoffmann et al. (2022), *Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models*, arXiv:2203.15556.

title: Predicting grokking time before generalization occurs
subfield: Scaling laws, grokking, and mechanistic explanations
open: Can we predict, from measurements taken early in training, both how long a network will take to generalize and whether it will generalize at all, on a specified family of algorithmic tasks? In other words, is there a transferable quantitative predictor of the onset time and probability of delayed generalization (grokking)?
status: Grokking was documented in 2022, and mechanistic progress measures exist for selected tasks, notably via mechanistic interpretability work in 2023. A transferable quantitative predictor remains an open target.
solved_when: A quantitative predictor, validated across a specified family of algorithmic tasks, forecasts from early training measurements both the onset time and the probability of delayed generalization.
why: It would distinguish productive long training from futile memorization, telling practitioners when persistence will pay off.
key_works: Power et al. (2022), *Grokking*, arXiv:2201.02177; Nanda et al. (2023), *Progress Measures for Grokking via Mechanistic Interpretability*, arXiv:2301.05217.

title: Genuine emergence versus measurement artifacts
subfield: Scaling laws, grokking, and mechanistic explanations
open: Are the "emergent abilities" reported in large language models genuine discontinuities in underlying capability, or artifacts of how we measure them? Designing preregistered experiments that can separate real capability transitions from apparent ones introduced by thresholded metrics, finite test sets, or task aggregation would settle this.
status: Schaeffer, Miranda, and Koyejo (2023), *Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?* (arXiv:2304.15004) demonstrated that metric choices alone can induce apparent emergence; Srivastava et al. Whether any particular claimed transition is genuinely structural remains open and requires a separate measurement design.
solved_when: A preregistered experimental design exists that can discriminate, for a given claimed emergence transition, whether the discontinuity persists once thresholded metrics, finite-test-set effects, and task aggregation are controlled for — and applying it yields a defensible verdict for that transition.
why: It would make claims about sudden capability growth scientifically discriminating, rather than unfalsifiable assertions that depend on arbitrary measurement choices.

title: Unknown-target soft interventions
open: Can causal structure over latent mechanisms be identified when we observe data from multiple environments that differ, but we are never told which mechanisms were soft-intervened on or how? A sharper form: give an identification theory, with finite-sample guarantees, for causal discovery under unknown soft interventions on unknown subsets of latent mechanisms.
status: This is currently a research target rather than an established result. The key conceptual point is that knowing which mechanism changed is a strictly stronger assumption than observing only that environments differ; the literature on causal representation learning (Schölkopf et al. 2021, *Towards Causal Representation Learning*, arXiv:2102.11107) and invariant-prediction causal inference (Peters, Bühlmann, and Meinshausen 2016, arXiv:1501.01332) provides the backdrop, but identification under unknown-target soft interventions remains open.
solved_when: A method is given that recovers the causal structure (up to the appropriate equivalence class induced by soft interventions) from multi-environment data without intervention labels, together with finite-sample guarantees.
why: Natural experiments and observational environments rarely come with intervention labels, so existing identification results that assume known intervention targets do not apply to the data actually available.
key_works: Schölkopf et al. (2021), *Towards Causal Representation Learning*, arXiv:2102.11107; Peters, Bühlmann, and Meinshausen (2016), *Causal Inference Using Invariant Prediction*, arXiv:1501.01332.

title: Worst-group learning with noisy or missing group labels
subfield: Robustness, domain shift, and performative effects
open: Can we learn a predictor with provable worst-group accuracy when the group labels themselves are unreliable — observed only partially or with noise, and with groups that overlap? More precisely, what are sharp bounds on the worst-group risk under such group uncertainty?
status: This is a research target. Group-distributionally robust optimization with known groups (Sagawa et al. (2020), *Distributionally Robust Neural Networks for Group Shifts*, arXiv:1911.08731) supplies a baseline, but group uncertainty changes identifiability and sample requirements; benchmarks such as WILDS (Koh et al. (2021), arXiv:2012.07421) motivate the setting.
solved_when: Sharp (identifiability-aware) worst-group risk guarantees are established for the setting of partially observed or noisy group labels with overlapping groups, including the corresponding sample-complexity requirements.
why: The vulnerable groups an application should protect may not be cleanly annotated; without guarantees under group uncertainty, robustness and fairness methods trained on imperfect group labels may silently fail exactly the populations they aim to protect.
key_works: Sagawa et al. (2020), *Distributionally Robust Neural Networks for Group Shifts*, arXiv:1911.08731; Koh et al. (2021), *WILDS*, arXiv:2012.07421.

title: Optimal conformal inference with estimated density ratios
open: Can conformal prediction retain valid coverage and near-optimal efficiency when the covariate-shift density ratio is estimated from finite data rather than known — even if the estimate is misspecified? Formally, the goal is sharp finite-sample guarantees for weighted conformal inference that explicitly account for estimation error and misspecification of the weights.

solved_when: A method with provable guarantees exists whose coverage and efficiency bounds are sharp (matching lower bounds) under estimated, possibly misspecified density ratios, with the guarantees quantified in terms of the finite-sample estimation error of the ratio.
why: Exact deployment-to-training density ratios are almost never available, so current theory that treats weights as known does not cover real deployments; guarantees robust to estimated weights are what make covariate-shift conformal methods dependable in practice.
key_works: Tibshirani, Barber, Candès, and Ramdas (2019), *Conformal Prediction Under Covariate Shift*, arXiv:1904.06019.

open: Can we unlearn data from a large trained model exactly — matching the output distribution that retraining without the deleted data would produce — at a fraction of the cost? title: Auditable certificates of unlearning
open: Can we construct certificates that let any third party independently verify, without retraining, that a machine-learning deletion procedure actually unlearned what it claimed — meeting a formally specified retraining-equivalence or approximate-unlearning guarantee?
status: This is a proposed target with no existing construction. Empirically, failure of a membership-inference attack is not itself proof that unlearning succeeded. Related machinery exists in verifiable computation (cryptography) and proof-carrying state updates (formal methods); key works include Neel et al. (2021), *Descent-to-Delete*, arXiv:2007.02923, and Sekhari et al. (2021), arXiv:2103.03279.
solved_when: A deletion procedure emits a certificate that an independent verifier can check against a formal retraining-equivalence or approximate-unlearning specification, without rerunning the original training.
why: It would make unlearning claims auditable: regulators, courts, or users could verify deletion was genuine rather than trusting the model owner's word.
key_works: Neel et al. (2021), *Descent-to-Delete*, arXiv:2007.02923; Sekhari et al. (2021), arXiv:2103.03279.

title: Computational cost of replicable learning
open: Which concept classes that are learnable in polynomial time can also be learned by polynomial-time replicable algorithms, and how does the required computational cost depend on the replication probability and accuracy parameters? In other words, characterize the efficient learnable classes that admit efficient replicable learners, with sharp dependence on replication probability and accuracy.
status: Replicability became a formal learning-theoretic program in 2022, initiated by Impagliazzo, Lei, Pitassi, and Sorrell (2022), *Reproducibility in Learning*, arXiv:2201.08430. It is known that statistical existence of replicable learners need not imply an efficient reproducible algorithm, but a full computational characterization remains open.
solved_when: A characterization is given of the efficiently learnable classes admitting efficient replicable learners, together with sharp bounds on how the replication probability and accuracy parameters enter the computational cost.
why: It tells us when two independent datasets drawn from the same distribution can be guaranteed to support the same operational decision, rather than merely achieving similar average risk — the property scientific replication actually demands.
key_works: Impagliazzo, Lei, Pitassi, and Sorrell (2022), *Reproducibility in Learning*, arXiv:2201.08430.

title: Identifiable operator discovery with unknown forcing
subfield: Scientific machine learning and operator learning
open: Which differential operators can actually be identified from finitely many noisy trajectories when the forcing, boundary conditions, or latent state variables are only partially observed? Formally, characterize the identifiability conditions under which the governing operator is uniquely determined despite unobserved inputs or hidden components.
status: This is currently a research target. The state of the art shows that accurately fitting observed trajectories does not uniquely identify the governing operator, so existing operator-learning approaches such as DeepONet (Lu et al., arXiv:1910.03193) and the framework of Kovachki et al. (2023), arXiv:2108.08481, do not by themselves resolve identifiability. Related literature spans PDE identifiability in inverse problems and unknown-input reconstruction in system identification.
solved_when: A characterization exists — stated in terms of the observation structure (which of forcing, boundary conditions, latent states are observed) and the noise level on the finite trajectories — that determines exactly when the governing operator is uniquely recoverable, distinguishing genuine identification from mere trajectory fitting.
why: It would separate genuine scientific discovery from flexible interpolation of measurements, telling us when a learned operator reflects the underlying physics rather than the capacity of the model to fit data.
key_works: Lu et al., *DeepONet: Learning Nonlinear Operators for Identifying Differential Equations*, arXiv:1910.03193; Kovachki et al. (2023), arXiv:2108.08481.

title: Efficient proper learning of structured quantum states
open: Which physically meaningful families of quantum states can be both predicted from few measurements and efficiently reconstructed as an actual state within the same family? Formally, identify broad classes for which sample-efficient PAC prediction and computationally efficient proper learning coincide.
status: PAC learnability of quantum states is established in an appropriate predictive sense (Aaronson 2007, *The Learnability of Quantum States*, arXiv:quant-ph/0608142, DOI:10.1098/rspa.2007.0113), and further developments appear in Huang, Kueng, and Preskill (2020), arXiv:2002.08953. Proper, computationally efficient reconstruction remains a stronger, unmet requirement.
solved_when: An explicitly described, physically meaningful family of quantum states is shown to admit sample-efficient prediction and polynomial-time proper reconstruction producing a state in that same family.
why: A predictor that answers measurement queries does not by itself give a usable state description; efficient proper reconstruction would yield states ready for simulation or quantum control.
key_works: Aaronson (2007), *The Learnability of Quantum States*, arXiv:quant-ph/0608142, DOI:10.1098/rspa.2007.0113; Huang, Kueng, and Preskill (2020), arXiv:2002.08953.

title: Distribution shifts with documented generating mechanisms
open: Can we build a benchmark of distribution shifts in which each shift comes with a documented generating mechanism, so that observed performance failures can be traced to specific violated assumptions?
status: This is a proposed extension beyond ordinary shift benchmarks; WILDS (Koh et al., 2021, arXiv:2012.07421) already supplies important real-world shift datasets.
solved_when: A benchmark exists whose shifts include recorded causal mechanisms, intervention metadata, and stable task definitions, sufficient to test specific theories of distribution shift.
why: A performance drop alone does not reveal which distributional assumption failed; mechanism documentation makes failures attributable and shift theories falsifiable.
key_works: Koh et al. (2021), *WILDS: A Benchmark of in-the-Wild Distribution Shifts*, arXiv:2012.07421; Peters et al. (2016), arXiv:1501.01332.

title: Ground-truth memorization and rule-learning benchmark
open: Can we build a suite of tasks in which a network can succeed either by memorizing ground-truth labels or by learning an underlying rule, with independent control over which solution is available, so that interpretability methods can be evaluated on whether they correctly identify which solution a trained model actually uses?
status: Currently a proposed benchmark target with no existing comprehensive construction. Grokking datasets (Power et al. (2022), *Grokking*, arXiv:2201.02177; Nanda et al. (2023), arXiv:2301.05217) provide a starting point but not a comprehensive ground-truth mechanism census.
solved_when: A benchmark exists containing tasks with separately controllable memorization and algorithmic solutions, published training checkpoints, and measurements of which solution is causally used by the trained models.
why: It would let researchers test claims about compression, generalization, and reasoning against known alternatives, rather than against unknown internal mechanisms.
key_works: Power et al. (2022), *Grokking*, arXiv:2201.02177; Nanda et al. (2023), arXiv:2301.05217.

title: Learning a defensible individual-fairness metric
open: Can we learn the similarity metric that individual fairness requires, rather than assuming it? Given explicit normative constraints and comparison data about which individuals should be treated alike, the question is whether a task-specific similarity metric can be learned with identifiable meaning and generalization guarantees.
status: The individual-fairness framework assumes a task-relevant metric; deriving and validating that metric is a separate research problem. The foundational framework is due to Dwork, Hardt, Pitassi, Reingold, and Zemel (2012), *Fairness Through Awareness*, arXiv:1104.3913, while related threads include social choice work on eliciting normative preferences and metric-learning work on identifiability from comparisons.
solved_when: A method exists that takes normative constraints and comparison data as input and outputs a task-specific similarity metric whose meaning is identifiable and which comes with provable generalization guarantees.
why: "Treat similar people similarly" is operational only when similarity is justified rather than silently chosen; without a defensible metric, the individual-fairness framework rests on an unexamined assumption.
key_works: Dwork, Hardt, Pitassi, Reingold, and Zemel (2012), *Fairness Through Awareness*, arXiv:1104.3913.

title: Multicalibration under endogenous outcomes
open: Can a predictor remain multicalibrated across subgroups when acting on its own predictions changes the very outcomes it forecasts — and even who belongs to which group? The question is to develop a notion of calibration that is robust to such feedback, with explicit bounds on how much calibration can degrade under performative deployment.
status: This is an open research target combining multicalibration (Hébert-Johnson, Kim, Reingold, and Rothblum, 2018, *Calibration for the Computationally-Identifiable Masses*, arXiv:1711.08513) with performative prediction (Perdomo et al., 2020, *Performative Prediction*, arXiv:2002.06673); it is known that static calibration need not be preserved after intervention.
solved_when: A prediction-and-intervention scheme is given that maintains subgroup calibration after deployment-induced distribution shift, together with quantitative bounds on feedback-induced calibration failure; no numeric targets are specified in the record, so the natural criterion for this problem type applies.
why: A forecast used to allocate resources can alter the event it was calibrated to predict, so static calibration guarantees silently break exactly when predictions matter most.
key_works: Hébert-Johnson, Kim, Reingold, and Rothblum (2018), *Calibration for the Computationally-Identifiable Masses*, arXiv:1711.08513; Perdomo et al. (2020), *Performative Prediction*, arXiv:2002.06673.

title: Computing learning coefficients for deep singular models
open: Can we compute, or sharply bound, the real log canonical threshold and the associated learning coefficients for explicit families of deep networks whose parameters are nonidentifiable? In Watanabe's singular learning theory, these quantities replace the parameter count as the measure of a model's effective complexity, so the question is what their exact values are for concrete deep architectures.
status: Singular learning theory explains why ordinary parameter counting fails for such models, but obtaining explicit learning coefficients for complex architectures remains an open target. The foundational framework is due to Watanabe (2013), *A Widely Applicable Bayesian Information Criterion*, JMLR 14:867–897, and Watanabe (2010), *Asymptotic Equivalence of Bayes Cross Validation and Widely Applicable Information Criterion in Singular Learning Theory*; the relevant mathematics draws on log canonical thresholds in algebraic geometry and resolution of singularities in singularity theory.
solved_when: For a specified family of deep networks with nonidentifiable parameters, the real log canonical threshold (and related learning coefficients) is computed exactly or bounded sharply, with the result holding for that architecture in the asymptotic Bayesian framework.
why: These coefficients govern the asymptotic Bayesian evidence and generalization behavior of singular models, so explicit values would turn Watanabe's general theory into usable model comparison and complexity estimates for real deep architectures.
key_works: Watanabe (2013), *A Widely Applicable Bayesian Information Criterion*, JMLR 14:867–897; Watanabe (2010), *Asymptotic Equivalence of Bayes Cross Validation and Widely Applicable Information Criterion in Singular Learning Theory*.

title: Polynomial-time uniform-distribution DNF learning
open: Can arbitrary polynomial-size DNF formulas be learned efficiently from random labeled examples alone? That is, is there a polynomial-time algorithm that learns any polynomial-size DNF over the uniform distribution on the Boolean cube using only random examples, without membership queries?
status: A longstanding problem from the early PAC-learning era. Restricted DNF families and stronger access models admit better algorithms; the general random-example target remains unresolved. Key works include Klivans and Servedio (2001) on subexponential DNF learning (DOI:10.1145/380752.380809) and Lecomte and Tan (2021), *Sharper Bounds on the Fourier Concentration of DNFs*, arXiv:2109.04525.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm learns arbitrary polynomial-size DNF formulas from random labeled examples under the uniform Boolean distribution, with no membership queries.
why: It is a central test of whether simple Boolean representations are computationally learnable, and it sits at the crossroads of circuit complexity and pseudorandomness.
key_works: Klivans and Servedio (2001), work on subexponential DNF learning, DOI:10.1145/380752.380809; Lecomte and Tan (2021), *Sharper Bounds on the Fourier Concentration of DNFs*, arXiv:2109.04525.

title: Exact logarithmic factors in discrete conditional-independence testing
open: In discrete conditional-independence testing, are the polylogarithmic factors in current sample-complexity bounds an artifact of the analysis, or genuinely required? A resolution would either remove these factors or prove them necessary across the relevant alphabet-size and accuracy regimes.
status: The principal polynomial sample-complexity gaps for both \(\ell_1\) and KL formulations were closed in 2026; the sharper question of an up-to-polylogarithms resolution remains open. (Seyfried, Mishra, Sen, and Tomamichel (2026), *Optimal Sample Complexity Lower Bounds on Conditional Independence Testing*, PMLR 336:5828–5873.)
solved_when: Conditional-independence tests over discrete alphabets whose sample complexity matches the known lower bounds up to constants — no polylogarithmic gaps in alphabet size or accuracy — or a proof that polylogarithmic overhead is unavoidable in those regimes.
why: Logarithmic factors can dominate the sample cost of tests with many conditioning categories, so tightening them directly determines when such tests are practical at scale.
key_works: Seyfried, Mishra, Sen, and Tomamichel (2026), *Optimal Sample Complexity Lower Bounds on Conditional Independence Testing*, PMLR 336:5828–5873.

title: Tenfold reduction in total hyperparameter-search cost
open: Can we cut the total computation spent tuning hyperparameters by at least \(10\times\), counting everything—failed runs, pilots, and the cost of transferring information across tasks—while still matching the quality that a strong full-scale search would achieve on a preregistered suite of models and tasks? In other words, the metric is end-to-end search cost, not just the cost of the runs that eventually succeed, and the comparison baseline is a strong full-scale search evaluated within a stated quality tolerance.
status: Currently a proposed moonshot with no solution. Zero-shot hyperparameter transfer, as in Yang et al. (2022), *Tensor Programs V: Tuning Large Neural Networks via Zero-Shot Hyperparameter Transfer* (arXiv:2203.03466), offers a concrete starting mechanism, but the target is stricter than existing methods account for, since it requires failures, pilot runs, and transfer overhead to be counted toward the budget. Related directions include multi-fidelity optimization via cheap proxy experiments and operations-research work on search-budget allocation.
solved_when: On a preregistered model-and-task suite, a method achieves at least a \(10\times\) reduction in total tuning computation relative to a strong full-scale search baseline, with all failures, pilot runs, and transfer overhead included in the accounting, while matching that baseline within a stated quality tolerance.
why: Hyperparameter tuning can consume resources comparable to or greater than the final training run itself, so a tenfold cut in search cost would directly free a large fraction of total training resources.
key_works: Yang et al. (2022), *Tensor Programs V: Tuning Large Neural Networks via Zero-Shot Hyperparameter Transfer*, arXiv:2203.03466.

title: Tenfold data reduction through verified learned structure
open: Can we show, in a rigorous matched-risk experiment, that exploiting learned invariances or representations genuinely reduces the labeled data a learner needs by a factor of ten? The structure must be discovered from the data itself, with no privileged task information leaking in.
status: A proposed target with no demonstration yet. Existing representation and invariance theories (e.g., HaoChen et al. (2021), arXiv:2106.04156; Soleymani et al. (2026), *Efficient Learning and Symmetry Discovery under Exact Invariances*) motivate the mechanism, but the required measurement must count the data used to discover the structure.
solved_when: A demonstrated \(10\times\) reduction in independently acquired labeled data attributable to learned invariances or representations, with no privileged task information and matched end-to-end risk, counting all data used to discover the structure.
why: It would quantify genuine learning-to-learn gains rather than merely relocating supervision into pretraining or benchmark design.
key_works: HaoChen et al. (2021), arXiv:2106.04156; Soleymani et al. (2026), *Efficient Learning and Symmetry Discovery under Exact Invariances*.

title: Fixed-parameter tractability of zonotope noncontainment
open: Is there a fixed-parameter tractable algorithm, with dimension as the parameter, for deciding zonotope noncontainment — or does some parameterized-complexity lower bound rule this out? status: Posed as an explicit 2025 problem by Froese et al. (2025), *Open Problem: Fixed-Parameter Tractability of Zonotope Problems*, separate from norm maximization. Related areas include polytope containment in computational geometry and geometric decision problems in parameterized complexity.
solved_when: Either an FPT algorithm for zonotope noncontainment parameterized by dimension is given, or an appropriate parameterized lower bound is proved.
why: It would clarify the dimensional barrier in exact neural verification, and connects to positivity and comparison of piecewise-linear functions.

title: Removing the remaining simultaneous U-calibration overhead
open: Can a single forecast sequence be simultaneously optimal for all bounded proper losses at once — attaining \(O(\sqrt T)\) regret for every such loss while improving to \(O(\log T)\) for every bounded smooth proper loss — with no extra logarithmic factor left in the general-loss guarantee?
status: As of 2026, a single algorithm (Frongillo, Luo, Mehta, and Schneider (2026), *Toward Simultaneously Optimal Regret in U-Calibration*) achieves the smooth-loss logarithmic rate together with a \(\widetilde O(\sqrt T)\) general bound, leaving only the logarithmic gap in the general-loss guarantee.
solved_when: A single forecasting algorithm achieves \(O(\sqrt T)\) U-calibration regret for every bounded proper loss and \(O(\log T)\) regret for every bounded smooth proper loss, eliminating the logarithmic overhead currently present in the general bound.
why: It determines whether universal forecasts can adapt optimally to all downstream decision-makers simultaneously, rather than paying a overhead penalty for generality.
key_works: Frongillo, Luo, Mehta, and Schneider (2026), *Toward Simultaneously Optimal Regret in U-Calibration*.

title: Can signed stepsizes beat nonnegative Silver exponents?
open: Can allowing negative stepsizes in a predetermined gradient-descent schedule improve the optimal convergence exponent beyond what nonnegative schedules achieve, in both fixed-horizon and anytime settings? Formally, determine the optimal convergence exponent for predetermined GD schedules permitted to use signed stepsizes.
status: As of September 2026, lower bounds beyond the classical first-order barrier are known for signed stepsizes, but the sharper Silver-exponent optimality result is stated only for nonnegative schedules (Ye and Liu (2026), *Improved Gradient Descent Lower Bounds Beyond Nesterov*, arXiv:2609.02855; *Silver Rate Is (Almost) Optimal*, arXiv:2609.09152).
solved_when: The optimal convergence exponent for signed, predetermined stepsize schedules is characterized (upper and lower bounds matching) in both the fixed-horizon and anytime settings, resolving whether it improves on the nonnegative (Silver-exponent) rate.
why: It answers whether temporarily moving against the gradient fundamentally enlarges the optimization power of stepsize-only methods, rather than merely permitting the same rates with different schedules.
key_works: Ye and Liu (2026), *Improved Gradient Descent Lower Bounds Beyond Nesterov*, arXiv:2609.02855; *Silver Rate Is (Almost) Optimal*, arXiv:2609.09152.

title: Necessary overparameterization for alternating least squares
open: For rank-\(r\), order-three tensor decomposition from random initialization, is superlinear overparameterization actually necessary for alternating least squares to provably succeed — or can ALS succeed with only \(k=o(r^2)\) fitted components?
status: Explicit COLT 2026 problem. A cited positive result works with \(k=O(r^2)\); the gap to smaller ranks is unresolved.
solved_when: A proof (positive or negative) resolves whether ALS from random initialization provably succeeds with \(k=o(r^2)\) components for rank-\(r\), order-three tensor decomposition, or a lower-bound argument showing \(k\) must be superlinear in \(r\).
why: Fewer fitted components would cut the memory, computation, and interpretability costs of tensor learning; the answer delineates what alternating minimization fundamentally requires.
key_works: Arvanitakis, Srinivas, and Vijayaraghavan (2026), *Open Problem: How Much Overparametrization Is Needed for ALS in Tensor Decomposition?*

title: Linear recursive teaching dimension
open: Is a concept class that can be learned from few random examples always teachable from comparably few well-chosen ones? Formally, is the recursive teaching dimension of every finite binary concept class bounded by \(O(d)\), where \(d\) is its VC dimension?
status: The problem has been studied since the early 2010s and was explicitly posed at COLT 2015 (Simon and Zilles, 2015, *Open Problem: Recursive Teaching Dimension Versus VC Dimension*). A general \(O(d^2)\) upper bound is known (Hu et al., 2017, *Quadratic Upper Bound for Recursive Teaching Dimension of Finite VC Classes*, arXiv:1702.05677), and some classes are known to require more than \(d\). Earlier work includes Doliwa et al. (2014), *Recursive Teaching Dimension, VC-Dimension and Sample Compression*.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) that the recursive teaching dimension of every finite binary concept class is \(O(d)\) in its VC dimension \(d\), improving on the known \(O(d^2)\) bound.
why: It would tightly connect statistical learnability and teachability, showing that the number of carefully chosen examples a teacher needs is governed by the same dimension that controls learning from random samples; a negative answer would separate the two notions.
key_works: Doliwa et al. (2014), *Recursive Teaching Dimension, VC-Dimension and Sample Compression*; Simon and Zilles (2015), *Open Problem: Recursive Teaching Dimension Versus VC Dimension*; Hu et al. title: DS-dimension product laws
open: How does the DS dimension of a product of multiclass hypothesis classes depend on the DS dimensions and structure of its factors — are there sharp formulas or necessary-and-sufficient structural bounds? The question asks for laws, not just upper or lower bounds in isolation.

solved_when: A characterization (exact formula, or tight structural condition) of the DS dimension of products of multiclass hypothesis classes is obtained, matching known bounds for the factors.
why: Such laws would let one derive structured-prediction sample complexity from reusable components, rather than recomputing it for each composite class.
key_works: Hanneke et al. (2024), *Open Problem: Direct Sums in Learning Theory*; Pabbaraju (2026), *The Optimal Sample Complexity of Multiclass and List Learning*, arXiv:2604.24749.

title: Tensor type-2 inequalities in the remaining norm regime
open: Does a type-2 inequality for Gaussian series of order-\(r\) tensors hold in the injective \(\ell_p\) norm throughout the remaining range \(2\le p<2r\)? A proof or refutation of the proposed bound settles the question.
status: The problem is explicitly catalogued in the 2025 Randomstrasse problems (Bandeira et al. (2026), *Randomstrasse101: Open Problems of 2025*, arXiv:2603.29571). The complementary regime \(p\ge 2r\) already has supporting results.
solved_when: The proposed type-2 bound for Gaussian order-\(r\) tensor series measured in injective \(\ell_p\) norm is established or refuted for all \(2\le p<2r\).
why: Such inequalities control the random tensor fluctuations underlying estimation and high-order learning methods, so settling them directly bounds the noise behavior of those procedures.

title: Structural characterization of agnostic direct-sum risk
open: Which structural properties of a hypothesis class govern how hard it is to agnostically learn its \(r\)-fold direct sum under whole-vector zero–one loss? Formally, one seeks invariants beyond the base class's minimax rate that characterize the direct-sum learning rate.
status: The question, posed by Hanneke, Moran, and Waknine (2024) in *Open Problem: Direct Sums in Learning Theory*, cannot be answered from the base class's minimax rate alone: More, Das, and Gupta (2026), *A Rate Separation for Agnostic Direct Sums* (arXiv:2608.06951), exhibit classes with identical base rates but different direct-sum rates.
solved_when: A structural invariant (or set of invariants) of the base class is identified that provably determines the agnostic learning rate of its \(r\)-fold direct sum under whole-vector zero–one loss, explaining the known rate separations.
why: It would let one predict the statistical cost of learning several outputs jointly rather than independently, separating when joint learning helps, hurts, or is unavoidable.
key_works: Hanneke, Moran, and Waknine (2024), *Open Problem: Direct Sums in Learning Theory*; More, Das, and Gupta (2026), *A Rate Separation for Agnostic Direct Sums*, arXiv:2608.06951.

title: Quantitative uniform estimation on product spaces
open: What is the sharp sample complexity for uniform estimation on product spaces? More precisely, how does it depend linearly on the VC dimension, the number of coordinates, the accuracy parameter, and the distribution's departure from independence?
status: A 2026 theorem by Holzman, Moran, and Shlimovich (*Uniform Laws of Large Numbers in Product Spaces*, arXiv:2603.24493) characterizes qualitative estimability under absolute continuity relative to the product of marginals; the quantitative bounds are explicitly left for further work.
solved_when: A characterization of the sample complexity is obtained, with matching (up to constants) upper and lower bounds expressed in terms of the VC dimension, number of coordinates, accuracy, and the deviation from independence of the underlying distribution.
why: It would make statistically tractable classes with infinite ordinary VC dimension usable in learning.
key_works: Holzman, Moran, and Shlimovich (2026), *Uniform Laws of Large Numbers in Product Spaces*, arXiv:2603.24493.

title: Computational characterization beyond DS dimension
open: Which multiclass classes with finite DS dimension can actually be learned in polynomial time, once the class is given by an explicit representation and we are allowed optimization-oracle access? Equivalently, characterize when the statistical characterization of multiclass learnability admits an efficient implementation.
status: This is currently a research target. The statistical characterization and optimal dimension dependence have advanced through 2026, notably via Brukhim et al. (2022), *A Characterization of Multiclass Learnability* (DOI:10.1109/FOCS54457.2022.00093) and Pabbaraju (2026), *The Optimal Sample Complexity of Multiclass and List Learning* (arXiv:2604.24749); however, these results do not themselves provide efficient implementations for arbitrary represented classes.
solved_when: A characterization — necessary and sufficient conditions on the represented class and oracle model under which every class of finite DS dimension admits a polynomial-time learner — is proven, with any stated quantitative dimension-dependence matching the known statistical sample complexity.
why: It separates the mere existence of a learner from implementable multiclass learning, determining whether finite DS dimension is a guarantee of efficient learnability or only of information-theoretic learnability.
key_works: Brukhim et al. (2022), *A Characterization of Multiclass Learnability*, DOI:10.1109/FOCS54457.2022.00093; Pabbaraju (2026), *The Optimal Sample Complexity of Multiclass and List Learning*, arXiv:2604.24749.

title: Characterizing compressible list-learnable classes
open: Which list-learnable classes admit bounded sample compression, and can these be characterized structurally — in particular, how do the permitted output-list size and the compression reconstruction shape the answer?
status: A blanket list analogue of the compression conjecture is false: even three-label, two-list-learnable examples can fail to be compressible (Hanneke, Moran, and Waknine (2026 version), *List Sample Compression and Uniform Convergence*, arXiv:2403.10889).
solved_when: A structural characterization exists of list-learnable classes that admit bounded sample compression, explicitly accounting for the role of the permitted output-list size and compression reconstruction.
why: It would identify exactly which ambiguous prediction problems support finite training certificates, sharpening where compression-based learnability arguments apply.
key_works: Hanneke, Moran, and Waknine (2026 version), *List Sample Compression and Uniform Convergence*, arXiv:2403.10889.
