title: Fourier entropy–influence conjecture
open: Does every Boolean function have Fourier entropy at most a constant multiple of its total influence — that is, \(H(\widehat f^2)\le C\,I(f)\) for a universal constant \(C\)? In other words, can the spectral description length of a Boolean function always be controlled by its sensitivity to bit flips?
status: This is the Friedgut–Kalai conjecture from 1996. Many structured classes and weaker general inequalities are known; O'Donnell and Tan (2013) established a composition theorem for the conjecture, Han (2025) gave a new bound (*A New Bound for the Fourier-Entropy-Influence Conjecture*, arXiv:2312.08271), and González, MacManus, and Pereyra (2026) supplied further evidence (*Further Evidence Towards the Fourier Entropy-Influence Conjecture*, arXiv:2606.00246) rather than a general proof.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the inequality \(H(\widehat f^2)\le C\,I(f)\) for all Boolean functions with a universal constant \(C\).
why: A positive answer would tightly connect a function's sensitivity to the length of its Fourier description, with consequences for learning low-influence functions.
key_works: O’Donnell and Tan (2013), *A Composition Theorem for the Fourier Entropy-Influence Conjecture*; Han (2025), *A New Bound for the Fourier-Entropy-Influence Conjecture*, arXiv:2312.08271; González, MacManus, and Pereyra (2026), *Further Evidence Towards the Fourier Entropy-Influence Conjecture*, arXiv:2606.00246.

title: Distribution-independent SQ learning versus linear dimension
open: Does every concept class that is efficiently learnable with statistical queries in a distribution-independent setting admit a low-dimensional linear representation — an appropriately small linear feature map — that carries comparable learning guarantees? In other words, is any distribution-independent SQ advantage of nonlinear learners necessarily tied to small dimension complexity?
status: Posed explicitly as a COLT 2026 open problem by Feldman, Kamath, and Srebro (2026), *Invited Open Problem: Is the Power of Deep Learning over Linear Models Inherently Distribution Dependent?*, PMLR 336:7117–7122. It connects communication-complexity notions of sign rank and dimension complexity with statistical-query separations from complexity theory; no resolution is recorded.
solved_when: Every efficiently distribution-independent SQ-learnable class is shown to admit a linear feature representation of appropriately small dimension whose learning guarantees are comparable to those of the original class; a negative answer exhibits an efficiently learnable class with no such small-dimension linear representation.
why: A positive answer would sharply restrict the distribution-independent advantage of nonlinear learning over linear models, confining any such benefit to settings that are inherently distribution dependent.
key_works: Feldman, Kamath, and Srebro (2026), *Invited Open Problem: Is the Power of Deep Learning over Linear Models Inherently Distribution Dependent?*, PMLR 336:7117–7122.

title: When low-degree failure predicts all efficient algorithms
open: Does the failure of low-degree polynomial methods to solve a planted inference problem reliably signal hardness for all efficient algorithms? State and prove a broadly applicable, nonvacuous theorem connecting low-degree failure to computational hardness for a precisely delimited family of planted inference models.
status: Low-degree analysis successfully predicts many thresholds, but it is not an unconditional characterization of all efficient inference; the problem remains a research target. See Kunisky, Wein, and Bandeira (2019), *Notes on Computational Hardness of Hypothesis Testing: Predictions Using the Low-Degree Likelihood Ratio*, arXiv:1907.11636.
solved_when: Such a theorem is stated and proved: broadly applicable, nonvacuous, and covering a precisely delimited family of planted inference models.
why: It would convert a powerful diagnostic into a reliable foundation for computational lower bounds.
key_works: Kunisky, Wein, and Bandeira (2019), *Notes on Computational Hardness of Hypothesis Testing: Predictions Using the Low-Degree Likelihood Ratio*, arXiv:1907.11636.

title: Many-community SBM algorithms in the remaining density regimes
open: Can we efficiently recover a large number of small communities in a stochastic block model with \(K\ge\sqrt n\) communities at the conjectured threshold, in graph-density regimes beyond those handled by current matching algorithms? More precisely: construct polynomial-time algorithms achieving the conjectured efficient recovery threshold across the density regimes not yet covered.
status: As of 2026, low-degree lower bounds cover all densities, while matching polynomial-time algorithms cover only the sparse and moderately sparse regimes; see Carpentier, Giraud, and Verzelen (2026), *Phase Transition for Stochastic Block Model with More than \(\sqrt n\) Communities*, PMLR 336:938–1000.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm achieves the conjectured efficient recovery threshold for \(K\ge\sqrt n\) in every graph-density regime where existing matching algorithms do not already apply, with matching low-degree lower bounds delimiting the computational gap.
why: It would clarify when many small communities can be recovered efficiently, rather than treating the classical fixed-\(K\) threshold as universal.
key_works: Carpentier, Giraud, and Verzelen (2026), *Phase Transition for Stochastic Block Model with More than \(\sqrt n\) Communities*, PMLR 336:938–1000.

title: Efficient graph alignment beyond convex-relaxation thresholds
open: What is the true polynomial-time recovery threshold for correlated Gaussian graph alignment? In particular, can efficient algorithms succeed in noise regimes where the standard doubly stochastic and hypercube relaxations fail?
status: A 2026 analysis locates the transition of the doubly stochastic and hypercube relaxations near \(n^{-1/2}\), up to logarithmic factors; this is not a threshold for all efficient algorithms. Key work: Massoulié, Varma, Vassaux, and Waldspurger (2026), *Phase Transition in Convex Relaxations for Graph Alignment*, PMLR 336:4999–5020.
solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm (or a proof of impossibility) is given that pins down recovery in correlated Gaussian graph alignment beyond the noise regime where standard doubly stochastic or hypercube relaxations succeed — i.e., beyond the transition near \(n^{-1/2}\), up to logarithmic factors, established for those relaxations.
why: It would improve matching of noisy networks, relational datasets, and latent correspondences.
key_works: Massoulié, Varma, Vassaux, and Waldspurger (2026), *Phase Transition in Convex Relaxations for Graph Alignment*, PMLR 336:4999–5020.

title: Generic complex phase retrieval below \(4M-4\) measurements
open: For generic complex phaseless measurements with \(N=4M-5\), what is the probability that the measurement map is injective up to global phase, and how does this probability behave asymptotically as \(M\) grows?
status: The old universal necessity of \(4M-4\) measurements is false. A refined 2025 open-problem formulation asks about the probability and asymptotics of exceptional injective configurations; see Bandeira et al. (2026), *Randomstrasse101: Open Problems of 2025*, arXiv:2603.29571, discussing the refined Vinzant phase-retrieval questions.
solved_when: The probability of injective phase retrieval at \(N=4M-5\) generic complex measurements is determined, together with its asymptotic behavior as \(M\to\infty\).
why: It would sharpen identifiability limits for phaseless sensing and latent inverse problems.
key_works: Bandeira et al. (2026), *Randomstrasse101: Open Problems of 2025*, arXiv:2603.29571, discussing the refined Vinzant phase-retrieval questions.

title: Robust regression’s full sample–condition-number–runtime frontier
open: Can we characterize the full tradeoff curve for robust regression with contaminated Gaussian designs and unknown covariance, matching upper and lower bounds on prediction error as a function of sample size, corruption rate, condition number, and computational budget?
status: A 2026 near-linear-time method uses roughly \(d/\epsilon^4\) samples and achieves \(O(\sqrt{\epsilon\kappa})\) prediction error when \(\epsilon\kappa\lesssim1\); significant tradeoff gaps remain. Key work: Adil, Błasiok, Chen, and Sridharan (2026), *On Efficient Robust Regression with Subquadratic Samples*, PMLR 336:3–74.
solved_when: Prediction-error bounds are achieved that match information-theoretic or computational lower bounds across sample size, corruption rate, condition number, and runtime; in particular, improving on or matching the current frontier of roughly \(d/\epsilon^4\) samples, \(O(\sqrt{\epsilon\kappa})\) prediction error for \(\epsilon\kappa\lesssim1\), in near-linear time.
why: It would guide robust regression in regimes where accurately estimating the covariance is itself expensive, telling practitioners exactly what accuracy is achievable at a given sample and compute budget.
key_works: Adil, Błasiok, Chen, and Sridharan (2026), *On Efficient Robust Regression with Subquadratic Samples*, PMLR 336:3–74.

title: Optimal Gaussian robust estimation beyond restricted algorithms
open: Can the information-theoretically optimal contamination dependence for high-dimensional Gaussian estimation be achieved by an efficient algorithm in the regimes not already ruled out for statistical query algorithms?
status: A longstanding statistical–computational gap remains open. SQ lower bounds — notably Diakonikolas, Kane, and Stewart (2017), *Statistical Query Lower Bounds for Robust Estimation of High-dimensional Gaussians and Gaussian Mixtures*, arXiv:1611.03473 — provide substantial evidence of hardness, but leave the power of more general algorithms unresolved.
solved_when: An efficient (e.g., polynomial-time) estimator attains the information-theoretically optimal contamination dependence for high-dimensional Gaussian estimation outside the regimes excluded by SQ lower bounds, or a matching general-algorithm lower bound closes the gap.
why: It determines whether the logarithmic or polynomial overheads currently incurred by robust estimation are inherent, pinning down the true computational cost of robustness.
key_works: Diakonikolas, Kane, and Stewart (2017), *Statistical Query Lower Bounds for Robust Estimation of High-dimensional Gaussians and Gaussian Mixtures*, arXiv:1611.03473.

title: Testable noise assumptions beyond Gaussian halfspaces
open: Which combinations of concept classes and marginal distributions admit a polynomial-time learner that can test its own noise assumption and, whenever the test accepts, certify near-optimal prediction? Formally, characterize the pairs (class, marginal family) for which such testable learning with certification is achievable in polynomial time.
status: Testing became tractable for Gaussian marginals with halfspaces under Massart noise, in work by Goel, Klivans, Stavropoulos, and Vasilyan (2026), *Testing Noise Assumptions of Learning Algorithms*, PMLR 336:2804–2853; the same work shows testability can be computationally harder than ordinary learning. Beyond the Gaussian-halfspace case, no characterization is known.
solved_when: A characterization exists of the concept classes and marginal families for which polynomial-time testing plus certified near-optimal prediction is possible — including an account of when testability is computationally harder than ordinary learning.
why: It would let learners replace unverifiable modeling assumptions with acceptance tests that actually certify prediction quality, making robust guarantees meaningful in practice rather than conditional on hope.
key_works: Goel, Klivans, Stavropoulos, and Vasilyan (2026), *Testing Noise Assumptions of Learning Algorithms*, PMLR 336:2804–2853.

title: Constant-factor optimality of the Silver rate
open: For gradient descent with predetermined nonnegative stepsizes on smooth convex functions, is the Silver schedule optimal up to a constant factor? Formally, close the subpolynomial gap between the Silver upper bound and the best general lower bound.
status: Results as of September 2026 determine the polynomial exponent \(p=\log_2(1+\sqrt2)\), so the exponent itself is no longer open; however, the lower bound retains an \(n^{-o(1)}\)-type loss. Key works: Altschuler and Parrilo (2025), *Acceleration by Stepsize Hedging I*, arXiv:2309.07879; Ye and Liu (2026), *Silver Rate Is (Almost) Optimal for Gradient Descent Acceleration*, arXiv:2609.09152.
solved_when: A matching upper and lower bound up to constant factors for predetermined nonnegative GD stepsizes on smooth convex functions is established, eliminating the current \(n^{-o(1)}\)-type loss separating the lower bound from the Silver rate with exponent \(p=\log_2(1+\sqrt2)\).
why: It would settle whether any asymptotic improvement remains beyond the Silver schedule.
key_works: Altschuler and Parrilo (2025), *Acceleration by Stepsize Hedging I*, arXiv:2309.07879; Ye and Liu (2026), *Silver Rate Is (Almost) Optimal for Gradient Descent Acceleration*, arXiv:2609.09152.

title: Sharp anytime GD rates beyond polynomial exponents
open: Can we pin down the exact convergence rate of gradient descent under nonnegative stepsize schedules that perform well at every stopping horizon, obtaining matching constant-factor or sharp logarithmic-factor bounds rather than only the leading polynomial exponent?
status: Anytime acceleration was established in 2024 (Zhang, Lee, Du, and Chen (2024), *Anytime Acceleration of Gradient Descent*, arXiv:2411.17668), and the optimal polynomial exponent was identified by 2026 lower bounds (Ye and Liu (2026), *Silver Rate Is (Almost) Optimal*, arXiv:2609.09152); finer asymptotics remain the target.
solved_when: For infinite predetermined nonnegative schedules that must work at every stopping horizon, matching upper and lower bounds are proved up to a constant factor, or up to a sharp logarithmic factor.
why: Real training often stops at an unplanned horizon rather than at a schedule's specially selected endpoint, so the true anytime rate determines what performance can be promised in practice.
key_works: Zhang, Lee, Du, and Chen (2024), *Anytime Acceleration of Gradient Descent*, arXiv:2411.17668; Ye and Liu (2026), *Silver Rate Is (Almost) Optimal*, arXiv:2609.09152.

title: Exact strongly convex stepsize complexity
open: What is the exact condition-number dependence of gradient descent with predetermined nonnegative stepsizes on strongly convex objectives? Closing this would pin down the remaining subpolynomial gap between the strongly convex Silver-schedule upper bounds and the universal lower bounds for such schedules.
status: September 2026 work matches the polynomial exponent of \(\kappa\), with lower complexity \(\kappa^{1/p-o(1)}\log(1/\delta)\); the exact dependence is the remaining refinement. Key work: Liu and Ye (2026), *Silver Rate Is (Almost) Optimal for Gradient Descent: The Strongly Convex Case*, arXiv:2609.26873.
solved_when: The exponent of \(\kappa\) in the stepsize complexity is determined exactly, matching the current upper bound \(\kappa^{1/p-o(1)}\log(1/\delta)\) up to the precise subpolynomial term.
why: It would establish the precise price of avoiding momentum in ill-conditioned optimization.
key_works: Liu and Ye (2026), *Silver Rate Is (Almost) Optimal for Gradient Descent: The Strongly Convex Case*, arXiv:2609.26873.

title: Finite-precision stability of aggressive schedules
open: Which accelerated stepsize schedules actually keep their speed when arithmetic is imperfect? The goal is sharp convergence and error-floor bounds for accelerated schedules under bounded or stochastic numerical error in each gradient evaluation and update.
status: This is a proposed theory target. Exact-arithmetic acceleration does not itself certify robustness to quantization, rounding, or mixed-precision accumulation. Key works: Altschuler and Parrilo (2025), *Acceleration by Stepsize Hedging I*; Zhang et al. (2024), *Anytime Acceleration of Gradient Descent*, arXiv:2411.17668.
solved_when: Provable convergence rates and error floors are established for accelerated stepsize schedules assuming each gradient and update carries bounded or stochastic numerical error, certifying robustness to quantization, rounding, and mixed-precision accumulation.
why: It would determine which provable accelerations survive implementation on low-precision hardware.
key_works: Altschuler and Parrilo (2025), *Acceleration by Stepsize Hedging I*; Zhang et al. (2024), *Anytime Acceleration of Gradient Descent*, arXiv:2411.17668.

title: Practically checkable convergence conditions for Adam
open: What practically checkable conditions on the loss geometry, gradient noise, and moment parameters characterize the regimes where standard Adam actually works? Formally, find such conditions that both explain Adam's successful regimes and can be verified without presupposing Adam's convergence.
status: This is currently a research target. General convergence of Adam is known to be false, and while modified algorithms and conditional convergence theorems exist, none provides a complete practical criterion. Key work: Reddi, Kale, and Kumar (2018), *On the Convergence of Adam and Beyond*, arXiv:1904.09237.
solved_when: A set of conditions on loss geometry, gradient noise, and moment parameters is identified that explains standard Adam's successful regimes and is checkable without assuming Adam's convergence.
why: It would replace optimizer folklore with conditions tied to observable training behavior, giving practitioners a principled basis for choosing Adam.
key_works: Reddi, Kale, and Kumar (2018), *On the Convergence of Adam and Beyond*, arXiv:1904.09237.

title: Boundary complexity in discontinuous online optimization
open: Which sequences of piecewise-Lipschitz objectives can be optimized with efficient sublinear regret, when the answer depends sharply on the geometry of the discontinuity boundaries rather than only on worst-case discretization?
status: The problem is posed as an explicit 2026 open-problem program, motivated by data-driven algorithm configuration, in Balcan, Pegden, and Sharma (2026), *Invited Open Problem: Online Optimization of Piecewise-Lipschitz Functions with Applications to Data-Driven Algorithm Design*.
solved_when: A characterization exists of the piecewise-Lipschitz objective sequences admitting efficient sublinear-regret algorithms, with regret bounds reflecting the discontinuity geometry rather than only worst-case discretization.
why: Algorithm performance often changes discontinuously with hyperparameters, so ordinary smooth optimization theory fails precisely in the data-driven algorithm-configuration settings where it is most needed.
key_works: Balcan, Pegden, and Sharma (2026), *Invited Open Problem: Online Optimization of Piecewise-Lipschitz Functions with Applications to Data-Driven Algorithm Design*.

title: Reparameterization-invariant complexity with predictive power
open: Can we define a complexity measure for neural networks that is provably invariant under any reparameterization leaving the implemented function unchanged, yet still predicts generalization behavior? The target is a single tractable quantity that simultaneously is invariant, yields useful risk bounds, and distinguishes successful from unsuccessful training.
status: This remains an open research target. Existing norm-based, flatness-based, and capacity-based measures each capture some relevant aspect of generalization, but none jointly satisfies the specification of invariance together with predictive risk bounds and the ability to distinguish training outcomes; see Berner, Grohs, Kutyniok, and Petersen (2021), *The Modern Mathematics of Deep Learning*, arXiv:2105.04026, and Nagarajan and Kolter (2019), arXiv:1902.04742.
solved_when: A complexity measure is constructed that (i) is invariant under function-preserving reparameterizations, (ii) yields nontrivial risk bounds, and (iii) empirically or theoretically separates successful from unsuccessful training runs.
why: Any complexity-based explanation of generalization that shifts merely because equivalent parameters are rescaled cannot be a genuine property of the learned function, so it fails as a scientific account of why networks generalize.
key_works: Berner, Grohs, Kutyniok, and Petersen (2021), *The Modern Mathematics of Deep Learning*, arXiv:2105.04026; Nagarajan and Kolter (2019), arXiv:1902.04742.

title: Benign overfitting with dependent training observations
open: When can a model overfit dependent training data — such as stationary mixing time series whose feature dimension grows — and still generalize well? The goal is to characterize necessary-and-sufficient conditions for benign overfitting under such specified dependent designs.
status: This is an open research target extending the independent-design theory of benign overfitting. Current understanding is that dependence alters the effective information and the interplay between covariance spectra and noise. Key works: Bartlett et al. (2020), *Benign Overfitting in Linear Regression*, arXiv:1906.11300; Holzman et al. (2026), *Uniform Laws of Large Numbers in Product Spaces*, arXiv:2603.24493.
solved_when: A precise criterion (necessary and sufficient) for benign overfitting is established for a specified dependent design, such as stationary mixing time series with growing feature dimension.
why: Most sequential, spatial, and repeated-user datasets are not independent samples, so the existing independent-design theory does not apply directly; dependence changes the effective information and the interaction between covariance spectra and noise.
key_works: Bartlett et al. (2020), *Benign Overfitting in Linear Regression*, arXiv:1906.11300; Holzman et al. (2026), *Uniform Laws of Large Numbers in Product Spaces*, arXiv:2603.24493.

title: Generalization certificates for the entire tuning procedure
open: Can we certify the population risk of the model a tuning pipeline actually outputs, taking into account the whole adaptive path that produced it — architecture search, optimizer tuning, checkpoint selection, and repeated validation access — rather than just the final checkpoint?
status: Proposed target. Adaptive-data-analysis theory controls information reuse, but obtaining tight certificates for large realistic tuning pipelines remains a distinct challenge. Key works: Dwork et al. (2015), *Generalization in Adaptive Data Analysis and Holdout Reuse*, arXiv:1506.02629; Dziugaite and Roy (2017), arXiv:1703.11008.
solved_when: A method yields tight generalization certificates for large, realistic tuning pipelines that account for adaptive architecture search, optimizer tuning, checkpoint selection, and repeated validation access.
why: Certifying a fixed checkpoint while ignoring how it was selected can understate overfitting, so current post-hoc guarantees may be misleading for adaptively tuned models.
key_works: Dwork et al. (2015), *Generalization in Adaptive Data Analysis and Holdout Reuse*, arXiv:1506.02629; Dziugaite and Roy (2017), arXiv:1703.11008.

title: Implicit bias of adaptive stochastic optimizers
subfield: Neural optimization dynamics and implicit bias
open: Which predictor does an adaptive stochastic method such as Adam actually select when trained on a separable nonlinear model? The question is to characterize the implicit bias that emerges from the interplay of stochastic noise, moment estimates, and per-parameter scaling.
status: This is currently a research target. The implicit bias of ordinary gradient descent is well understood in important homogeneous settings, but the implicit bias of practical adaptive stochastic training remains far less clear. Key works: Soudry et al. (2018), arXiv:1710.10345; Reddi, Kale, and Kumar (2018), *On the Convergence of Adam and Beyond*, arXiv:1904.09237.
solved_when: A characterization is given of the predictor selected by Adam-like adaptive stochastic methods on separable nonlinear models, accounting for the joint effect of stochastic noise, moment estimates, and parameter scaling.
why: It would connect the choice of optimizer directly to the learned function, rather than to convergence speed alone.
key_works: Soudry et al. (2018), arXiv:1710.10345; Reddi, Kale, and Kumar (2018), *On the Convergence of Adam and Beyond*, arXiv:1904.09237.

title: Finite-width thresholds for feature learning
subfield: Neural optimization dynamics and implicit bias
open: For specified multi-index teacher models, how narrow can a network be — and how long must it train — before standard randomly initialized SGD escapes kernel-like behavior and genuinely learns features? Formally, the goal is to determine the smallest width and training time at which feature learning, rather than effective kernel regression, takes hold.
status: This is currently a research target. Infinite-width feature-learning descriptions and 2026 vanilla-SGD limitations provide partial boundaries, not a complete finite-width phase diagram. Related pointers include Yang and Hu (2021), arXiv:2011.14522, and Barzilai and Shamir (2026), *Limitations of SGD for Multi-Index Models Beyond Statistical Queries*, with connections to dynamical phase transitions in statistical mechanics and signal emergence in random matrix theory.
solved_when: For specified multi-index teacher models, a characterization is given of the smallest network width and training time at which standard randomly initialized SGD learns useful features rather than remaining effectively kernel-like.
why: It would predict the parameter scale needed for genuine representation learning, telling practitioners how large a model must be before optimization does more than memorize through a kernel.
key_works: Yang and Hu (2021), arXiv:2011.14522; Barzilai and Shamir (2026), *Limitations of SGD for Multi-Index Models Beyond Statistical Queries*.

title: Joint depth–width–time limits
subfield: Neural optimization dynamics and implicit bias
open: What happens to neural network training dynamics when depth, width, and training time all grow together? The goal is a controlled joint limit for this simultaneous scaling, with explicit approximation errors bounding how finite networks deviate from the limit.
status: This is a research target. It is known that taking width to infinity while holding other quantities fixed does not automatically justify simultaneous scaling. Foundational infinite-width analyses include Yang and Hu (2021), *Feature Learning in Infinite-Width Neural Networks*, arXiv:2011.14522, and Yang et al. (2022), *Tensor Programs V*, arXiv:2203.03466.
solved_when: A joint limit theorem is derived in which depth, width, and training duration scale together, together with quantitative approximation errors for networks of finite depth, width, and training time.
why: Real models are made deeper, wider, and longer-trained at the same time, so single-parameter asymptotic theories do not describe their actual training regime.
key_works: Yang and Hu (2021), *Feature Learning in Infinite-Width Neural Networks*, arXiv:2011.14522; Yang et al. (2022), *Tensor Programs V*, arXiv:2203.03466.

title: Predictive theory of the edge of stability
subfield: Neural optimization dynamics and implicit bias
open: Can we predict, from measurable properties of a training problem, how gradient descent on a finite neural network will evolve — its curvature trajectory, loss oscillations, and eventual learning progress? In formal terms, the goal is a theory that derives these finite-step dynamics directly from identifiable features of the optimization setup.
status: The edge-of-stability phenomenon was documented in 2021 by Cohen et al. (2021), *Gradient Descent on Neural Networks Typically Occurs at the Edge of Stability*, arXiv:2103.00065. A broadly predictive, finite-network theory remains a research target.
solved_when: A predictive account exists that quantitatively forecasts the evolving curvature, loss oscillation behavior, and learning progress of finite-step neural gradient descent from measurable properties of the training problem.
why: It would explain why practical learning rates operate outside classical monotone-descent conditions.
key_works: Cohen et al. (2021), *Gradient Descent on Neural Networks Typically Occurs at the Edge of Stability*, arXiv:2103.00065.

title: Edge-of-stability dynamics with minibatching and preconditioning
subfield: Neural optimization dynamics and implicit bias
open: What quantity governs "edge-of-stability" behavior in neural network training once the idealizations of deterministic gradient descent are dropped? In other words, determine which curvature or generalized-stability quantity predicts training behavior when minibatch noise and adaptive preconditioning replace deterministic GD.
status: This is a research target extending deterministic observations (Cohen et al. (2021), arXiv:2103.00065; Reddi et al. (2018), arXiv:1904.09237). It is currently known that the Hessian's largest eigenvalue alone need not capture a history-dependent optimizer; related connections include stochastic dynamics with multiplicative noise and control theory on time-varying stability margins.
solved_when: A curvature or generalized-stability quantity is identified that provably predicts the training dynamics of history-dependent, preconditioned stochastic optimizers — showing that the Hessian's largest eigenvalue alone does not suffice — with the prediction matching observed edge-of-stability behavior in that setting.
why: Most large-scale training uses neither full-batch gradients nor an unchanging Euclidean metric, so the existing deterministic picture of edge-of-stability dynamics does not describe how real training actually behaves.
key_works: Cohen et al. (2021), arXiv:2103.00065; Reddi et al. (2018), arXiv:1904.09237.

title: Complete vanilla-SGD phase diagrams for multi-index models
subfield: Neural optimization dynamics and implicit bias
open: When a multi-index target is learned by plain, unmodified SGD, which combinations of signal structure, sample reuse, batch size, learning rate, and network architecture succeed? The goal is matching upper and lower bounds that together give a complete phase diagram for vanilla SGD in this setting.
status: A 2026 non-statistical-query framework yields new lower bounds for standard SGD and exposes shortcomings in older SQ-based predictions. Key work: Barzilai and Shamir (2026), *Limitations of SGD for Multi-Index Models Beyond Statistical Queries*, PMLR 336:559–612.
solved_when: For each configuration of signal structure, sample reuse, batch size, learning rate, and network architecture in multi-index models, matching upper and lower bounds on learnability by ordinary SGD are established.
why: It identifies what standard training can actually learn, with no algorithmic modifications hidden inside the theorem — a ground truth for which conclusions about SGD survive without extra machinery.
key_works: Barzilai and Shamir (2026), *Limitations of SGD for Multi-Index Models Beyond Statistical Queries*, PMLR 336:559–612.

title: Exact depth required to compute the maximum with ReLUs
open: How deep must an arbitrarily wide ReLU network be to compute the maximum of d real inputs exactly? More precisely, what is the minimum depth needed to represent max{x₁,…,x_d} exactly under a clearly specified depth convention?
status: A longstanding depth-separation problem. A 2026 result, Safran (2026), *A Depth Hierarchy for Computing the Maximum in ReLU Networks via Extremal Graph Theory*, PMLR 336, proves new superlinear width lower bounds at several depths, but not the full width-independent depth conjecture.
solved_when: The exact minimum depth required to represent max{x₁,…,x_d} with unrestricted-width ReLU networks is determined (upper and matching lower bound) under a clearly specified depth convention.
why: It isolates an elementary function whose exact neural depth complexity remains surprisingly subtle.

title: Sharp depth–width–precision tradeoffs
open: When a network must pay for depth, width, and the bit precision of its weights, how much of each does it take to approximate a given class of smooth compositional functions? In other words, characterize the full depth–width–precision resource tradeoff for such function classes.
status: This is currently a research target. Approximation results that count real-valued parameters alone do not determine implementable description complexity. Key works: Berner et al. (2021), *The Modern Mathematics of Deep Learning*, arXiv:2105.04026.
solved_when: A characterization exists of the resources (depth, width, and weight bit precision jointly) needed to approximate the specified smooth compositional function class to the required accuracy, with matching constructions and lower bounds.
why: It separates genuine representational efficiency from the artifact of encoding information into unrealistically precise weights, which existing real-parameter counts cannot detect.

title: Efficient discovery of approximate symmetries
open: Can we efficiently learn transformations that hold only approximately, when the underlying symmetry group is itself unknown, in a way that provably degrades continuously as the symmetry is increasingly violated?

solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm discovers and exploits approximately valid transformations for unknown symmetry groups, with guarantees that degrade continuously with the degree of symmetry violation.
why: Real data rarely satisfy the exact symmetries assumed by equivariant models, so a principled approximate theory would extend symmetry-based learning to practical data.

title: Verifiable expressivity without exhaustive input enumeration

title: Efficient sequential omniprediction under distribution change
open: Can a single forecaster, deployed once, remain simultaneously competitive for a large family of downstream proper losses when the data distribution changes over time? Formally, is there an efficient sequential omniprediction procedure whose regret adapts to a specified variation budget on the drift of contexts and outcome distributions?

solved_when: An explicit, computationally efficient algorithm exists that maintains omniprediction guarantees over a sequence of distribution changes, with regret bounded by a function of the specified variation budget.
why: A shared forecast should remain useful to different consumers — each with their own loss — as conditions evolve, rather than requiring a separately retrained predictor for every loss and every shift.
key_works: Gibbs and Tibshirani (2026), *Sample-Efficient Omniprediction for Proper Losses*; Gibbs and Candès (2021), *Adaptive Conformal Inference Under Distribution Shift*, arXiv:2106.00170.

open: Given a family of decision losses, what is the weakest calibration or moment condition on a predictor that still guarantees near-optimal decisions for every loss in the family — and can we match this with tight sample complexity?

title: Sharp learnability of nonstationary partial-monitoring games
open: When a learner receives only indirect feedback and the environment's losses drift over time under an explicit variation budget, what regret is achievable in partial-monitoring games? More precisely, can the known interactive-complexity classification be extended to give a sharp learnability criterion that unifies all nonstationary feedback structures?

General interactive complexity frameworks, such as Foster, Foster, Golowich, and Rakhlin (2023), *On the Complexity of Multi-Agent Decision Making: From Learning in Games to Partial Monitoring*, arXiv:2305.00684, cover important stationary or adversarial formulations, but they do not collapse all nonstationary feedback structures into one sharp criterion.
solved_when: A characterization of minimax regret for nonstationary partial-monitoring games under explicit variation constraints is proved, collapsing all nonstationary feedback structures into one sharp criterion matching the stationary theory in generality.
why: Many real systems observe only proxies, delayed signals, or the consequences of their own actions, so a sharp criterion tells us when such systems can learn at all — and at what rate — as their environments drift.

title: Learning changing strategic-response models
open: Can a predictor achieve meaningful regret guarantees when the very agents it predicts adapt to it, with manipulation costs and feasible responses that are unknown and change over time? In other words, is there a framework that learns the evolving strategic environment while cleanly separating the learner's observation of behavior from its influence on that behavior?
status: Research target. This is distinct from the older fixed-model strategic-classification regret question; the unresolved specification includes unknown, evolving response structure. solved_when: A learning algorithm is exhibited with provable regret guarantees for the setting where agents' manipulation costs or feasible response sets are unknown and time-varying, together with a formal separation between learning the environment and influencing it.
why: Predictors deployed in markets, admissions, or ranking systems change the behavior they observe, so guarantees that assume a fixed response model can silently fail exactly where such systems are used most.
key_works: Perdomo et al. (2020), *Performative Prediction*, arXiv:2002.06673; Foster et al. (2023), *On the Complexity of Multi-Agent Decision Making*, arXiv:2305.00684.

title: Sharp dimensional dependence in bandit convex optimization
open: What is the intrinsic price, in regret, of optimizing a high-dimensional convex function when the learner only observes scalar feedback? More precisely, determine matching minimax regret bounds — in both dimension and horizon — for specified stochastic or adversarial bandit-convex-optimization models.

solved_when: For a fixed model (with its assumptions made explicit), upper and lower minimax regret bounds are established that match in their dependence on dimension and on the horizon.
why: It quantifies the exact cost of dimension when learning to optimize from bandit feedback, pinning down which exploration strategies and rates are truly necessary rather than merely achievable.

title: Computable instance-optimal exploration allocations
open: Can we turn information-theoretically optimal exploration allocations into algorithms that a computer can actually run in polynomial time, for structured bandit classes where computing the allocation is itself hard? In other words, when does instance-optimal pure exploration admit a computationally efficient realization?

solved_when: For a structured bandit class whose optimal exploration allocation is difficult to compute, a polynomial-time algorithm is exhibited that matches the instance-optimal sample complexity of the information-theoretic allocation.
why: It would make instance-optimal sample efficiency operational rather than purely existential: practitioners could actually deploy allocations that today are known only through statistical characterizations.
key_works: Foster et al. (2021), *The Statistical Complexity of Interactive Decision Making*, arXiv:2112.13487; Chen et al. (2024), *Assouad, Fano, and Le Cam with Interaction*, arXiv:2410.05117.

title: Computationally efficient DEC-optimal reinforcement learning

status: Currently a research target. The DEC framework of Foster et al. (2021), *The Statistical Complexity of Interactive Decision Making*, arXiv:2112.13487, gives powerful statistical characterizations, but statistical complexity and computational tractability remain distinct questions.
solved_when: Broad model classes are identified for which DEC-optimal statistical guarantees are attained by polynomial-time algorithms using implementable estimation oracles.
why: It could unify provably efficient reinforcement learning without hiding the cost in expensive planning or model-selection subroutines.

title: Sharp rather than polynomial-factor interactive complexity
open: For interactive decision-making over specified convex model classes, can the remaining polynomial-factor gaps between the general lower-bound characterizations and the achievable regret or sample complexity be closed to obtain sharp constants? In other words, when does the unified interactive lower-bound machinery pin down the exact rate, not merely its order?

solved_when: For a specified convex model class, matching upper and lower bounds are established up to constant factors—no polynomial gap remains between the interactive lower-bound characterization and the achievable regret or sample complexity.
why: Polynomial-factor losses decide whether a theoretically learnable system is usable in practice, so sharp rates separate learnability in principle from learnability with realistic sample budgets.

title: Offline policy evaluation with unknown behavior policy
open: Given only trajectory data from an unknown behavior policy, when can a target policy's value still be estimated statistically efficiently in fixed-horizon offline RL? solved_when: A theorem (positive or negative) settles statistical efficiency of policy evaluation from trajectory data under linear \(q^\pi\)-realizability and concentrability, with the behavior policy unknown — matching the known-behavior-policy setting in guarantees.
why: Logged datasets often omit exact action propensities or were produced by changing systems, so evaluation methods that require knowing the behavior policy cannot be applied.
key_works: Tkachuk, Szepesvári, and Tan (2026), *Trajectory Data Suffices for Statistically Efficient Policy Evaluation in Fixed-Horizon Offline RL with Linear \(q^\pi\)-Realizability and Concentrability*.

title: Computational tractability of trajectory-based offline RL
open: Can the best statistically efficient guarantees for offline reinforcement learning from trajectory data be achieved by algorithms running in polynomial time, given explicit access to the relevant function classes? That is, does trajectory-based statistical efficiency translate into computational tractability?
status: Research target. It is known that trajectories can overcome certain statistical impossibilities that hold for unstructured transition samples, but this by itself does not settle computational efficiency. solved_when: A polynomial-time algorithm (with explicit function-class access) is shown to match the strongest known statistically efficient trajectory-based offline-RL guarantees, or such an implementation is ruled out under standard complexity assumptions.
why: It separates the statistical value of richer logs from the computational cost of processing them, clarifying when trajectory data genuinely helps.

title: Model-free DEC guarantees with realistic function approximation
open: Can model-free reinforcement learning attain DEC-style exploration guarantees using practical regression or representation-learning primitives, rather than requiring inaccessible optimization over abstract function classes?

why: It would connect unifying RL theory to actual value-based training systems.

why: It would quantify the information price of avoiding catastrophic experiments, telling us exactly how much harder safe exploration is than unconstrained exploration.

title: Sharp horizon dependence in imitation under distribution shift
open: How does the effective horizon penalty in behavior cloning actually behave once error rates, stability of the dynamics, and coverage of the expert's data distribution are specified jointly, rather than each bounded in isolation? A precise characterization would give the instance-optimal horizon dependence of imitation performance under distribution shift.

why: It would explain when supervised imitation alone suffices and when interactive data collection is necessary, replacing compounding-error folklore with a sharp criterion.

title: Reliable policy selection with learned, exploitable evaluators
open: When a policy search is allowed to adapt against an imperfect learned evaluator, how well does the selected policy actually perform on the true task? (2023), *On the Complexity of Multi-Agent Decision Making*, arXiv:2305.00684.
solved_when: A bound is obtained on true task performance of the selected policy under unrestricted adaptive policy improvement against an imperfect learned evaluator, covering correlated errors across candidate trajectories — not merely fixed candidate distributions or pairwise win-rate guarantees.
why: It treats reward hacking as a statistical interaction problem rather than merely an anecdotal failure, which is a prerequisite for principled analysis of evaluation-driven policy optimization.

title: Learning augmentations rather than assuming them

open: Can an augmentation mechanism be learned, rather than assumed, from unlabeled data alone? The goal is a method with provable guarantees that the learned augmentations preserve information relevant to downstream tasks and deliver a sample-efficiency gain, under explicit structural assumptions.

title: Global recoverability in nonlinear continual learning
subfield: Representation learning, active learning, and continual learning
open: When a network is trained sequentially on a stream of tasks, what structural conditions on the tasks and the parameterization guarantee that it still converges globally — not merely from initializations near a solution? Formally: find checkable conditions, going beyond local regularity, that ensure global convergence under sequential task training.
status: A 2026 analysis (Schliserman et al. (2026), *Convergence of Continual Learning in Homogeneous Deep Networks*) proves that global convergence can fail even in simple nonlinear parameterizations, while establishing local linear convergence under regularity assumptions.
solved_when: A set of checkable structural conditions is identified that guarantee global convergence of sequential task training, and these conditions provably go beyond the known local regularity assumptions that yield only local linear convergence.
why: It separates forgetting that can be recovered from irreversible drift into bad task-interaction states, telling us when continual-learning failures are fixable rather than permanent.
key_works: Schliserman et al. (2026), *Convergence of Continual Learning in Homogeneous Deep Networks*.

bib.title: Global recoverability in nonlinear continual learning

title: In-context adaptation to unseen task priors
open: How well can an in-context learner perform when deployed on task priors different from those seen during pretraining? Formally, quantify the risk of an in-context learner under a deployment task prior that differs from the pretraining prior, and characterize what adaptation is achievable from the prompt alone.
status: This is currently a research target. Existing task-family analyses often assume a specified training distribution, as in Bai et al. (2023), *Transformers as Statisticians*, arXiv:2306.04637, and Akyürek et al. (2023), *What Learning Algorithm Is In-Context Learning?*, arXiv:2211.15661.
solved_when: A theoretical characterization of the risk of an in-context learner under deployment task priors differing from the pretraining prior exists, together with results determining what adaptation is possible from the prompt alone.
why: Real users present task families not sampled from a model's pretraining experience, so risk guarantees that assume a matched prior fail exactly where deployment matters.
key_works: Bai et al. (2023), *Transformers as Statisticians*, arXiv:2306.04637; Akyürek et al. (2023), *What Learning Algorithm Is In-Context Learning?*, arXiv:2211.15661.

bib.title: In-context adaptation to unseen task priors

title: Robust in-context estimation with corrupted demonstrations
open: What estimation risk is achievable when a bounded fraction of the demonstrations in a prompt are adversarially corrupted — mislabeled, duplicated, or maliciously selected — and does standard training actually discover a robust estimator?
status: Currently a research target extending clean synthetic-task analyses of in-context learning, notably Garg et al. (2022), arXiv:2208.01066, and Akyürek et al. (2023), arXiv:2211.15661; connections run to contamination-resistant regression in robust statistics and to poisoned-exemplar attacks in security.
solved_when: A characterization of the achievable risk under a stated bounded corruption fraction is proved, together with a proof (positive or negative) of whether standard training discovers estimators attaining that risk.
why: Demonstrations in real prompts are neither guaranteed independent nor guaranteed correct, so clean-prompt guarantees do not transfer to practice without such a theory.
key_works: Garg et al. (2022), arXiv:2208.01066; Akyürek et al. (2023), arXiv:2211.15661.

bib.title: Robust in-context estimation with corrupted demonstrations

title: Finite-precision length generalization
open: Can we prove that a transformer trained on bounded-length sequences actually executes a specified algorithm on sequences longer than any it saw during training, once we account for finite numerical precision, error accumulation across positions, and the positional encoding? In other words, establish a guarantee of length generalization for a concrete learned algorithm under realistic finite-precision arithmetic.
status: This is currently an open research target; existing expressivity and finite-context learning guarantees do not imply unbounded length extrapolation. Key works: Yang, Srebro, and Li (2026), *Tight Sample Complexity of Transformers*; Giapitzakis et al. (2026), *On the Statistical Query Complexity of Learning Semiautomata*.
solved_when: A proof exists that the trained transformer implements the specified sequence algorithm on inputs beyond the training lengths, with the analysis explicitly handling bounded precision, accumulated numerical error, and the positional encoding scheme.
why: Such a result separates genuine algorithm learning from mere interpolation over familiar sequence lengths, which is what current expressivity and in-context learning theory cannot distinguish.
key_works: Yang, Srebro, and Li (2026), *Tight Sample Complexity of Transformers*; Giapitzakis et al. (2026), *On the Statistical Query Complexity of Learning Semiautomata*.

bib.title: Finite-precision length generalization

title: Computational learning complexity of bounded transformers
open: When a transformer's depth, number of heads, weight precision, and context length are all explicitly bounded and the data is drawn from a specified distribution, is finding a good predictor computationally efficient — or is there evidence of hardness? In other words, is efficient learnability or computational hardness decidable for such bounded transformers?
status: Nearly tight VC/sample-complexity results appeared in 2026 in Yang, Srebro, and Li (2026), *Tight Sample Complexity of Transformers*, PMLR 336; these do not settle the computational cost of finding a good predictor.
solved_when: A theorem establishes, for transformers with explicitly bounded depth, heads, weight precision, and context length under a specified data distribution, either a polynomial-time learning algorithm or a hardness result for finding a good predictor.
why: It separates datasets that are statistically adequate from architectures that are algorithmically learnable, clarifying which transformer classes can actually be learned efficiently rather than merely estimated well in principle.
key_works: Yang, Srebro, and Li (2026), *Tight Sample Complexity of Transformers*, PMLR 336.

bib.title: Computational learning complexity of bounded transformers

title: Learning semiautomata beyond statistical queries
open: Can semiautomata families that are hard to learn via statistical queries nevertheless be learned efficiently by algorithms outside the SQ model — or is there a broader computational hardness barrier?
status: A 2026 result proves SQ hardness under uniform words and initial states using transition structure rather than only parity-like output languages: Giapitzakis, Fountoulakis, Nichani, and Lee (2026), *On the Statistical Query Complexity of Learning Semiautomata: A Random Walk Approach*.
solved_when: Either an efficient non-SQ learning algorithm is given for the semiautomata families underlying the SQ hardness results, or a computational hardness result extending beyond the SQ setting is established.
why: It tests the limits of learning latent state-transition algorithms from sequences, determining whether SQ hardness reflects a genuine computational barrier or merely an artifact of the query model.
key_works: Giapitzakis, Fountoulakis, Nichani, and Lee (2026), *On the Statistical Query Complexity of Learning Semiautomata: A Random Walk Approach*.

bib.title: Learning semiautomata beyond statistical queries

title: Task-aware lower bounds for context compression
open: How much memory is truly required to preserve a transformer's answers under a specified query distribution, rather than preserving all token representations uniformly? Formally, this asks for task-aware lower bounds on the memory needed so that, over the given distribution of queries, the model's answers remain unchanged.
status: Proposed target; no results yet. General architecture sample complexity does not characterize the information that a particular downstream task must retain. Key works: Yang, Srebro, and Li (2026), *Tight Sample Complexity of Transformers*; Bai et al. (2023), arXiv:2306.04637.
solved_when: A lower bound (and ideally a matching construction) is established on the minimum memory sufficient to preserve a transformer's answers for the specified query distribution, characterizing what the downstream task must retain rather than what the full context contains.
why: It would give principled limits and concrete objectives for context and cache compression, replacing uniform preservation of all token representations with provably sufficient task-specific compression.
key_works: Yang, Srebro, and Li (2026), *Tight Sample Complexity of Transformers*; Bai et al. (2023), arXiv:2306.04637.

bib.title: Task-aware lower bounds for context compression

title: Joint training-and-inference compute optimality
subfield: Scaling laws, grokking, and mechanistic explanations
open: How should a system designer jointly allocate compute across model size, data volume, training duration, and inference-time computation, given a specified lifetime distribution of queries and a quality constraint? In formal terms, what allocation minimizes total lifetime compute subject to meeting the quality target over the expected query load?
status: Training-compute allocation has strong empirical baselines, notably Hoffmann et al. (2022), *Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models*, arXiv:2203.15556; joint lifetime optimization is a different target because inference demand changes the objective, and related work such as Sriraman and Block (2026), *Revisiting the Suboptimality of Best-of-N*, examines inference-time selection. Connections are noted to operations research on lifecycle resource allocation and economics on amortization of fixed costs.
solved_when: A method (theoretical or with strong empirical grounding) is given for choosing model size, data volume, training duration, and inference-time compute that provably or demonstrably minimizes total compute over the specified lifetime query distribution subject to the quality constraint.
why: The cheapest model to train need not be the cheapest system to operate, so training-only optimality can misallocate compute once inference demand shapes the objective.
key_works: Hoffmann et al. (2022), *Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models*, arXiv:2203.15556; Sriraman and Block (2026), *Revisiting the Suboptimality of Best-of-N*.

bib.title: Joint training-and-inference compute optimality

title: Scaling with redundant and adaptively reused data
subfield: Scaling laws, grokking, and mechanistic explanations
open: Can we predict how learning curves behave when training examples are correlated, duplicated, repeatedly replayed, or selected adaptively — replacing raw token count with a measurable notion of the information actually conveyed to the learner? Formally, the goal is a scaling law parameterized by a quantity of novel statistical information that uniquely determines expected performance under redundancy and adaptive reuse of data.
status: This remains a research target. The scaling-law literature, including Kaplan et al. (2020), arXiv:2001.08361 and Hoffmann et al. (2022), arXiv:2203.15556, fits curves with conventional scaling variables, but these do not uniquely measure novel statistical information; the problem is also connected to work such as Holzman et al. (2026), arXiv:2603.24493. No predictive theory for redundant or adaptively reused data currently exists.
solved_when: A measurable information-based quantity — computable from the data and training procedure — is shown to predict learning curves for correlated, duplicated, replayed, and adaptively selected data, where conventional fitted scaling variables fail to uniquely measure novel statistical information.
why: It would make it possible to decide quantitatively when collecting new data beats running additional epochs over existing data — a core cost tradeoff in training large models.
key_works: Kaplan et al. (2020), arXiv:2001.08361; Hoffmann et al. (2022), arXiv:2203.15556; Holzman et al. (2026), arXiv:2603.24493.

bib.title: Scaling with redundant and adaptively reused data

title: Identifiability of superposed features
subfield: Scaling laws, grokking, and mechanistic explanations
open: Under an explicit generative model, when are a learned representation’s constituent features uniquely recoverable, up to stated symmetries, from activations and interventions?
status: Toy superposition models expose useful mechanisms, but recovering a unique feature ontology from arbitrary activations is not guaranteed. Related work includes Elhage et al. (2022), *Toy Models of Superposition*, arXiv:2209.10652, and Locatello et al. (2019), arXiv:1811.12359; connections run to sparse coding (dictionary identifiability) and inverse problems (nonunique decompositions).
solved_when: A characterization is given of the conditions under which features are identifiable up to the stated symmetries, with a proof of uniqueness under those conditions and a demonstration of non-uniqueness when they fail.
why: It would clarify whether interpretability methods discover real structure or one of many equivalent decompositions.
key_works: Elhage et al. (2022), *Toy Models of Superposition*, arXiv:2209.10652; Locatello et al. (2019), arXiv:1811.12359.

bib.title: Identifiability of superposed features

title: Causally selective feature editing
subfield: Scaling laws, grokking, and mechanistic explanations
open: Can we edit a single identified internal feature of a model while provably leaving a specified set of unrelated behaviors intact over a defined input distribution? Formally, the task is to construct an intervention on the feature such that the target behavior changes as intended yet the unrelated behaviors are preserved on that distribution.
status: Proposed target with no existing solution. So far, finding a correlated feature or a successful local intervention does not establish selective causal control. Related ideas draw on causal inference (targeted interventions) and control theory (decoupling of system responses); key works include Elhage et al. (2022), *Toy Models of Superposition*, arXiv:2209.10652, and Nanda et al. (2023), arXiv:2301.05217.
solved_when: An intervention on an identified internal feature achieves the intended change while provably preserving the specified set of unrelated behaviors over the defined input distribution.
why: It would turn interpretability into controlled model repair, allowing targeted fixes rather than mere observation of internals.
key_works: Elhage et al. (2022), *Toy Models of Superposition*, arXiv:2209.10652; Nanda et al. (2023), arXiv:2301.05217.

bib.title: Causally selective feature editing

title: Completeness certificates for mechanistic explanations
subfield: Scaling laws, grokking, and mechanistic explanations
open: Can we certify that an extracted circuit genuinely explains a specified fraction of a model’s behavior — including under counterfactual interventions and on out-of-sample inputs — rather than merely showing it is influential? A formal certificate would establish that mechanisms omitted from the explanation are negligible, not just that those included play some role.
status: Currently a proposed target; no such certificate exists. The state of the art stops at demonstrating that a circuit is influential, which is strictly weaker than showing that omitted mechanisms are negligible. Key works: Nanda et al. (2023), *Progress Measures for Grokking via Mechanistic Interpretability*, arXiv:2301.05217; Ribeiro, Singh, and Guestrin (2016), *Why Should I Trust You?*, arXiv:1602.04938.
solved_when: A method exists that, for an extracted circuit, produces a checkable certificate quantifying the fraction of the model’s behavior it explains, where the account holds under counterfactual interventions and out-of-sample inputs, and omitted mechanisms are shown to be negligible.
why: Without such certificates, partial explanations can be mistaken for complete accounts of how a model works, undermining trust in mechanistic interpretability findings.
key_works: Nanda et al. (2023), *Progress Measures for Grokking via Mechanistic Interpretability*, arXiv:2301.05217; Ribeiro, Singh, and Guestrin (2016), *Why Should I Trust You?*, arXiv:1602.04938.

bib.title: Completeness certificates for mechanistic explanations

title: End-to-end computational complexity of score learning and sampling
subfield: Diffusion, flow matching, and generative learning
open: Can we prove end-to-end guarantees for diffusion-based generative modeling — that is, jointly bound the data required, the training computation to learn the score, and the sampling computation — for a concrete distribution family, rather than assuming access to accurate scores as a black box?
status: Guarantees for sampling given accurate scores are established, including Song et al. (2021), *Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations*, arXiv:2011.13456. Recent work by Chewi et al. (2026), *DDPM Score Matching and Distribution Learning*, connects score matching to density and parameter estimation. End-to-end computational optimality remains family-dependent and unresolved.
solved_when: Matching upper and lower bounds on total sample complexity, training-computation, and sampling-computation are established for a specified concrete distribution family, with learning the score included as part of the cost.
why: A fast sampler alone does not give a fast generative learner when estimating the score dominates the overall cost; without end-to-end bounds, sampling guarantees may be vacuous in practice.
key_works: Song et al. (2021), *Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations*, arXiv:2011.13456; Chewi et al. (2026), *DDPM Score Matching and Distribution Learning*.

bib.title: End-to-end computational complexity of score learning and sampling

title: Adaptive diffusion learning on unknown manifolds
subfield: Diffusion, flow matching, and generative learning
open: Can diffusion models be learned, end-to-end, at rates that adapt to data living on or near an unknown low-dimensional manifold? Formally, the goal is a sharp statistical and computational theory in which the estimator adapts to unknown intrinsic dimension, curvature, and noise thickness without paying unnecessary ambient-dimensional costs.
status: Low-dimensional diffusion theory has advanced through 2026, including work such as Chakraborty, Berthet, and Bartlett (2026), *Generalization Properties of Score-Matching Diffusion Models for Intrinsically Low-Dimensional Data*, arXiv:2603.03700, and Song et al. (2021), arXiv:2011.13456. The open target combines adaptation, geometric uncertainty, and computational guarantees rather than merely asking whether intrinsic-dimension results exist at all.
solved_when: End-to-end rates for diffusion learning are established that adapt to unknown intrinsic dimension, curvature, and noise thickness, with all ambient-dimensional costs removed beyond what is provably necessary.
why: High-dimensional observations often lie near much smaller latent spaces, so ambient-dimensional sample and compute costs are wasted capacity; a solution tells us when diffusion models can escape the curse of ambient dimension.
key_works: Chakraborty, Berthet, and Bartlett (2026), *Generalization Properties of Score-Matching Diffusion Models for Intrinsically Low-Dimensional Data*, arXiv:2603.03700; Song et al. (2021), arXiv:2011.13456.

bib.title: Adaptive diffusion learning on unknown manifolds

title: Tractable subclasses of Gaussian-mixture score learning
subfield: Diffusion, flow matching, and generative learning
open: Which structural conditions on a Gaussian mixture make its score learnable in polynomial time at statistically efficient accuracy? More precisely, characterize the subclasses of Gaussian mixtures for which efficient score matching succeeds despite the general-case intractability.
status: Positive mixture-learning results coexist with 2026 computational and cryptographic lower bounds for general score-estimation families. Key works: Chen, Kontonis, and Shah (2025), *Learning General Gaussian Mixtures with Efficient Score Matching*; Chewi et al. (2026), *DDPM Score Matching and Distribution Learning*. Related connections include algebraic statistics (mixture identifiability) and cryptography (hard distribution learning).
solved_when: A characterization is given of mixture conditions (e.g., on components or structure) under which score estimation is polynomial-time feasible at statistically efficient accuracy — or a proof that no such tractable subclass exists beyond the known positive cases.
why: It would separate realistic tractable mixture structure from impossible general-purpose promises, telling us when diffusion-style score matching is genuinely efficient rather than relying on unattainable guarantees.
key_works: Chen, Kontonis, and Shah (2025), *Learning General Gaussian Mixtures with Efficient Score Matching*; Chewi et al. (2026), *DDPM Score Matching and Distribution Learning*.

title: Certified few-step generative sampling
subfield: Diffusion, flow matching, and generative learning
open: Identify broad distribution classes admitting one-to-ten-step sampling with a rigorous distributional-error guarantee and account for the computation needed to learn the accelerated sampler.
status: Proposed quantitative target. Fast empirical generation does not itself establish distributional accuracy or end-to-end computational savings.
why: It could reduce generative inference latency and energy by an order of magnitude without hiding quality loss.
key_works: Ho, Jain, and Abbeel (2020), *Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models*, arXiv:2006.11239; Lipman et al. (2023), *Flow Matching for Generative Modeling*, arXiv:2210.02747.

title: Robust conditional guidance under score misspecification
subfield: Diffusion, flow matching, and generative learning
open: When a diffusion or flow-matching model is steered by conditional guidance, how much does any error in the underlying score estimate get amplified in the guided sampler? The goal is to characterize this amplification and to construct guidance rules with provable, certified tradeoffs between how well generated samples satisfy the conditioning constraint and how faithfully they match the intended conditional distribution.
status: This is currently a research target with no resolved results recorded. The state of the art consists of foundational and neighboring work: Song et al. (2021), arXiv:2011.13456, and Moitra, Risteski, and Rohatgi (2026), *Steering Diffusion Models with Quadratic Rewards: A Fine-Grained Analysis*. It is known that guarantees for an unconditional learned sampler do not automatically survive aggressive conditioning. Related perspectives come from rare-event simulation (importance-weight instability) and control theory (guided stochastic processes).
solved_when: A theory that quantifies how conditional guidance amplifies score-estimation error, together with guidance rules carrying certified tradeoffs between constraint satisfaction and distributional fidelity.
why: Many useful generation tasks require conditioning on rare or difficult constraints, and guarantees for an unconditional learned sampler do not automatically survive aggressive conditioning.
key_works: Song et al. (2021), arXiv:2011.13456; Moitra, Risteski, and Rohatgi (2026), *Steering Diffusion Models with Quadratic Rewards: A Fine-Grained Analysis*.

bib.title: Robust conditional guidance under score misspecification

title: Masked-diffusion scheduling with learnable structural knowledge
subfield: Diffusion, flow matching, and generative learning
open: What structural information about a target distribution can be learned efficiently and yet suffices to choose a near-optimal parallel unmasking schedule?
status: A 2026 characterization gives optimal schedules in principle, but it also proves that competing with them without strong prior information can be impossible.
solved_when: A class of learnable structural knowledge is identified that is efficiently learnable and provably sufficient to select a parallel unmasking schedule competitive with the optimal ones characterized in principle by Chen, Cong, and Li (2026).
why: It isolates the actual information needed to turn parallel token generation into a reliable speedup, rather than an empirical heuristic.
key_works: Chen, Cong, and Li (2026), *Optimal Inference Schedules for Masked Diffusion Models*.

bib.title: Masked-diffusion scheduling with learnable structural knowledge

title: Instance-optimal discrete diffusion beyond a fixed sampler family
subfield: Diffusion, flow matching, and generative learning
open: What is the true sampling cost of generating from structured discrete distributions when no restriction is placed on the sampler? A complete answer would characterize instance-optimal guarantees over all admissible samplers and clarify how information-adaptive \(\tau\)-leaping compares against this universal optimum.
status: In 2026, sharp bounds and algorithmic lower bounds were established for important discrete-diffusion samplers (Dmitriev, Huang, and Wei (2026), *Efficient Sampling with Discrete Diffusion Models: Sharp and Adaptive Guarantees*); however, these are not automatically universal lower bounds over every sampler.
solved_when: Sharp upper and lower bounds on the optimal sampling cost for structured discrete distributions hold over the class of all admissible samplers, and the relationship of these bounds to information-adaptive \(\tau\)-leaping guarantees is characterized.
why: It separates limitations of a particular discretization method from the intrinsic generative complexity of the distribution, showing which inefficiencies belong to the sampler rather than the problem.
key_works: Dmitriev, Huang, and Wei (2026), *Efficient Sampling with Discrete Diffusion Models: Sharp and Adaptive Guarantees*.

title: Optimal flow-matching couplings under a model-complexity budget
subfield: Diffusion, flow matching, and generative learning
open: Which choice of training coupling and probability path allows a finite-capacity flow model to reach a given generative target at the lowest total cost? Formally, the problem is to select couplings and paths that jointly minimize the sum of approximation, optimization, and numerical-integration costs for the model.
status: This remains a research target. The key observation is that a mathematically valid transport path need not be the easiest path for a given network to learn or integrate. Flow matching was introduced in Lipman et al. (2023), *Flow Matching for Generative Modeling*, arXiv:2210.02747; related perspectives come from optimal transport (dynamic transport cost) and numerical analysis (stiffness minimization).
solved_when: A principled criterion (and, ideally, a construction) identifies couplings and probability paths that minimize the combined approximation, optimization, and numerical-integration cost of a finite-capacity flow model, together with theory quantifying the achieved trade-off.
why: It would connect transport geometry directly to end-to-end generative efficiency, replacing heuristically chosen paths with complexity-aware ones.
key_works: Lipman et al. (2023), *Flow Matching for Generative Modeling*, arXiv:2210.02747.

title: Minimal interventions for latent causal identification
open: How few interventions — and of what kind — suffice to recover both the latent causal graph and its underlying variables from observations generated by an explicit nonlinear model? Formally, characterize the minimal intervention number and type required for identifiability of latent causal structure and representations under such an observation model.
status: Research target. Causal representation learning supplies positive identifiable regimes, but minimal intervention complexity depends strongly on the observation and intervention classes; see Schölkopf et al. (2021), *Towards Causal Representation Learning*, arXiv:2102.11107, and Khemakhem et al. (2020), arXiv:1907.04809.
solved_when: A characterization exists of the minimum number and type of interventions that identify a latent causal graph and its variables under an explicit nonlinear observation model, with matching positive (achievability) and negative (impossibility) results.
why: It would guide the design of experiments that reveal causal variables rather than merely predictive features.
key_works: Schölkopf et al. (2021), *Towards Causal Representation Learning*, arXiv:2102.11107; Khemakhem et al. (2020), arXiv:1907.04809.

bib.title: Minimal interventions for latent causal identification

title: Stable nonlinear-ICA identifiability
open: Can nonlinear ICA latents be provably recovered with sharp finite-sample guarantees when the auxiliary-variable assumptions that drive identifiability hold only weakly or approximately? In other words, turn the qualitative identifiability theory into quantitative bounds that remain meaningful outside the exactly-specified, infinite-data regime.
status: This is currently a research target; no such bounds are recorded. The state of the art is the unifying identifiability framework of Khemakhem, Kingma, Monti, and Hyvärinen (2020), *Variational Autoencoders and Nonlinear ICA: A Unifying Framework*, arXiv:1907.04809, which establishes identifiability but not finite-sample stability under weak or approximate auxiliary variation. Related threads exist in the conditioning of identification maps in inverse problems and stability in blind source separation.
solved_when: Recovery bounds for nonlinear-ICA identifiability are established that are finite-sample, and remain valid (quantitatively) when auxiliary variation is weak and the model assumptions are only approximately satisfied.
why: Identifiability in the infinite-data, correctly specified setting does not ensure numerically stable recovery; a solution would reveal whether theoretically identifiable latent variables can actually be estimated from available data.
key_works: Khemakhem, Kingma, Monti, and Hyvärinen (2020), *Variational Autoencoders and Nonlinear ICA: A Unifying Framework*, arXiv:1907.04809.

title: Transporting causal predictions with hidden confounding
open: Which causal or interventional predictions about a target environment can be identified from data collected across multiple source environments when some confounders remain unobserved? Formally, the goal is a characterization of the identifiable functionals in this multi-source, hidden-confounding transport setting.
status: This is an open research target. It is known that invariance alone does not resolve every transport problem, especially when the hidden mechanisms differ; see Peters et al. (2016), *Causal Inference Using Invariant Prediction*, arXiv:1501.01332, and Schölkopf et al. (2021), arXiv:2102.11107.
solved_when: A complete characterization exists of the target-environment causal or interventional predictions that are identifiable from multiple source environments in the presence of unobserved confounders.
why: It would determine when causal models genuinely support deployment beyond their training environment.
key_works: Peters et al. (2016), *Causal Inference Using Invariant Prediction*, arXiv:1501.01332; Schölkopf et al. (2021), arXiv:2102.11107.

title: Learning cyclic causal mechanisms from limited interventions
open: Can the feedback mechanisms of a nonlinear cyclic causal system — and the effects of interventions on it — be identified from only a limited number of perturbations? The question is whether, under explicit stability and functional assumptions, the cyclic structural mechanisms and their intervention responses are recoverable rather than merely the acyclic equilibrium distribution.
status: This is currently a research target: it is known that acyclic structural assumptions and equilibrium observations do not automatically identify dynamic feedback. Key works: Schölkopf et al. (2021), *Towards Causal Representation Learning*, arXiv:2102.11107; Perdomo et al. (2020), *Performative Prediction*, arXiv:2002.06673. Related threads include feedback identification in control theory and equilibrium-versus-transient causation in dynamical systems.
solved_when: A method or characterization exists that, under stated stability and functional assumptions, identifies the feedback mechanisms and intervention effects in nonlinear cyclic systems from limited perturbations, with a proof of identifiability (or a precise characterization of when identifiability fails).
why: Biological, economic, and controlled systems often contain feedback loops, so causal methods restricted to acyclic structure leave these domains without valid intervention predictions.
key_works: Schölkopf et al. (2021), *Towards Causal Representation Learning*, arXiv:2102.11107; Perdomo et al. (2020), *Performative Prediction*, arXiv:2002.06673.
