title: Useful partial identification of learned counterfactuals
open: Can we compute sharp, tractable bounds on counterfactual quantities when observational and interventional data narrow the true causal mechanism down only to an equivalence class of latent causal models? In other words, replace the common practice of picking one plausible generative model with a principled quantification of what every model in the identified class jointly implies about the counterfactual.
status: This is currently a research target. The state of the art is that selecting one plausible generative model from the identified class is common practice, but such a selection is not a certificate that its counterfactuals are uniquely determined. Related threads include partial identification in econometrics and decisions over model sets in robust optimization; key works are Schölkopf et al. (2021), arXiv:2102.11107 and Locatello et al. (2019), arXiv:1811.12359.
solved_when: A method exists that, given data identifying only an equivalence class of latent causal models, outputs counterfactual bounds that are both computationally tractable and sharp (i.e., achieve the tightest bounds consistent with the class).
why: It would replace unjustified point counterfactuals with honest, decision-relevant uncertainty, so downstream decisions rest on provable bounds rather than an arbitrary model choice.
key_works: Schölkopf et al. (2021), arXiv:2102.11107; Locatello et al. (2019), arXiv:1811.12359.

title: Cost-optimal adaptive causal experimentation
open: Can we learn an adaptive intervention policy that identifies a specified causal effect while minimizing the total cost of the experiments it performs, when interventions have heterogeneous costs and there is latent uncertainty about the underlying causal system? Formally, the goal is a policy whose cumulative experimental cost matches the cost-optimal sample complexity for identifying the target effect.
status: This is a research target at the intersection of causal identification and interactive decision complexity, connecting to causal discovery methods as in Peters et al. (2016), arXiv:1501.01332, and to the statistical complexity of interactive decision making as characterized by Foster et al. (2021), *The Statistical Complexity of Interactive Decision Making*, arXiv:2112.13487.
solved_when: An algorithm (with analysis) is given that adaptively selects interventions and, under heterogeneous intervention costs and latent uncertainty, identifies the specified causal effect with total experimental cost provably matching the optimal cost-aware benchmark up to stated approximation factors.
why: The most informative experiment may be expensive, unsafe, or impossible to repeat, so cost-blind identification procedures can be practically unusable; a cost-optimal policy would tell us which experiments are actually worth running.
key_works: Peters et al. (2016), arXiv:1501.01332; Foster et al. (2021), *The Statistical Complexity of Interactive Decision Making*, arXiv:2112.13487.

title: Distinguishing causal invariance from accidental stability
open: How can we tell whether a predictor that remains accurate across environments is genuinely invariant to the underlying causal mechanism, or merely stable by accident on the environments we happened to observe? Formally, the goal is to design tests that distinguish genuinely mechanism-preserving predictors from predictors that happen to remain accurate across the observed environments.
status: Currently a proposed target; no method exists. The core difficulty is that finitely many observed environments may fail to expose spurious invariances. Relevant background includes Peters et al. (2016), *Causal Inference Using Invariant Prediction*, arXiv:1501.01332, and Arjovsky et al. (2019), *Invariant Risk Minimization*, arXiv:1907.02893.
solved_when: A test or experimental design exists that reliably separates mechanism-preserving predictors from accidentally stable ones, including in cases where the finitely observed environments would otherwise fail to expose spurious invariances.
why: It would make claims of causal generalization falsifiable, turning invariance-based causal assertions from assumptions into testable hypotheses.
key_works: Peters et al. (2016), *Causal Inference Using Invariant Prediction*, arXiv:1501.01332; Arjovsky et al. (2019), *Invariant Risk Minimization*, arXiv:1907.02893.

title: Sharp robustness–accuracy frontiers for realistic generative models
subfield: Robustness, domain shift, and performative effects
open: For a concrete nonlinear data-generating model, what is the full frontier of achievable clean risk versus adversarial risk — and how does that frontier shift when the classifier is computationally bounded rather than arbitrarily powerful?
status: That a tension between robustness and accuracy exists is established, and the frontier is known to be model-dependent rather than a universal fixed penalty. Key works: Tsipras et al. (2019), *Robustness May Be at Odds with Accuracy*, arXiv:1805.12152; Bubeck, Price, and Razenshteyn (2018), *Adversarial Examples from Computational Constraints*, arXiv:1805.10204.
solved_when: A specified nonlinear data-generating model is paired with a characterization of its achievable clean-risk/adversarial-risk frontier under stated computational restrictions, together with matching achievability and impossibility results for that model.
why: It would separate tradeoffs that are information-theoretically unavoidable from artifacts of current training methods, telling us where better algorithms can still close the gap.
key_works: Tsipras et al. (2019), *Robustness May Be at Odds with Accuracy*, arXiv:1805.12152; Bubeck, Price, and Razenshteyn (2018), *Adversarial Examples from Computational Constraints*, arXiv:1805.10204.

title: Robust sample complexity with learned geometric structure
subfield: Robustness, domain shift, and performative effects
open: When does learning a data manifold or invariance structure reduce the additional samples needed for adversarial robustness? More precisely, characterize the settings in which structure-learning provably closes part of the sample-complexity gap between robust and standard generalization.
status: Robust generalization can require more data even in simple models, as shown by Schmidt et al. (2018), *Adversarially Robust Generalization Requires More Data*, arXiv:1804.11285. Whether structure-learning removes particular gaps remains a separate, model-specific question; Soleymani et al. (2026), *Efficient Learning and Symmetry Discovery under Exact Invariances*, addresses related symmetry learning.
solved_when: A characterization (theorem or counterexample) is given of the models in which learning a manifold or invariance structure reduces the additional sample cost of adversarial robustness, with the magnitude of any savings quantified.
why: It would identify when unlabeled or geometric information can substitute for costly robust labels.
key_works: Schmidt et al. (2018), *Adversarially Robust Generalization Requires More Data*, arXiv:1804.11285; Soleymani et al. (2026), *Efficient Learning and Symmetry Discovery under Exact Invariances*.

title: Certification for composed semantic transformations
subfield: Robustness, domain shift, and performative effects
open: Can we certify that a model's prediction is stable when an image undergoes a specified composition of geometric, photometric, and occlusion transformations — and can this be done with a perturbation model that is both sound and tractable?
status: Research target. Tight Gaussian smoothing certificates for \(\ell_2\) perturbations do not solve semantic-composition certification. Key works: Cohen, Rosenfeld, and Kolter (2019), *Certified Adversarial Robustness via Randomized Smoothing*, arXiv:1902.02918; Hendrycks and Dietterich (2019), *Benchmarking Neural Network Robustness to Common Corruptions and Perturbations*, arXiv:1903.12261.
solved_when: A certification method exists that provides sound guarantees of prediction stability under a specified composition of geometric, photometric, and occlusion transformations, with a tractable perturbation model covering such semantic transformations rather than only pixel-norm balls.
why: Pixel-norm guarantees may not cover the changes users regard as meaning-preserving, so current certificates can leave exactly the transformations people care about uncertified.
key_works: Cohen, Rosenfeld, and Kolter (2019), *Certified Adversarial Robustness via Randomized Smoothing*, arXiv:1902.02918; Hendrycks and Dietterich (2019), *Benchmarking Neural Network Robustness to Common Corruptions and Perturbations*, arXiv:1903.12261.

title: Finite-environment guarantees for domain generalization
subfield: Robustness, domain shift, and performative effects
open: How many distinct training environments, and of what diversity, are needed to guarantee good performance on an unseen environment drawn from a specified meta-distribution? More precisely, characterize the environment-complexity measure that governs sample-complexity-style guarantees in domain generalization.
status: This is currently a research target. It is known that guarantees against arbitrary unseen distributions are impossible without assumptions, and existing empirical protocols do not determine the right environment-complexity measure. Key works: Gulrajani and Lopez-Paz (2021), *In Search of Lost Domain Generalization*, arXiv:2007.01434; Arjovsky et al. (2019), *Invariant Risk Minimization*, arXiv:1907.02893.
solved_when: A theory identifies the number and diversity of training environments sufficient to guarantee a stated performance level on unseen environments drawn from the given meta-distribution, and shows which environment-complexity measure controls this.
why: More examples from a single environment may not substitute for observing more environments, so without such a theory practitioners cannot know when collecting additional environments is necessary and existing empirical protocols give no principled target.
key_works: Gulrajani and Lopez-Paz (2021), *In Search of Lost Domain Generalization*, arXiv:2007.01434; Arjovsky et al. (2019), *Invariant Risk Minimization*, arXiv:1907.02893.

title: Testable out-of-distribution detection guarantees
subfield: Robustness, domain shift, and performative effects
open: For which restricted families of distribution shift can a detector, given only training data and unlabeled deployment data, test its assumptions at deployment and still guarantee a meaningful tradeoff between false alarms and missed shifts?
status: This is currently a research target; no such characterization is known. The record notes that detecting every possible unseen distribution is not a meaningful unrestricted guarantee. Key works: Koh et al. (2021), *WILDS*, arXiv:2012.07421; Goel et al. (2026), *Testing Noise Assumptions of Learning Algorithms*. Related directions include hypothesis testing with composite alternatives and change detection at detectability boundaries.
solved_when: A characterization exists of shift families admitting such tests, together with guarantees on the false-alarm versus missed-shift tradeoff; unrestricted detection of every possible unseen distribution is explicitly excluded as not meaningful.
why: It would make abstention and monitoring guarantees conditional on explicit, inspectable assumptions rather than unverifiable claims about all possible distributions.
key_works: Koh et al. (2021), *WILDS*, arXiv:2012.07421; Goel et al. (2026), *Testing Noise Assumptions of Learning Algorithms*.

title: Learning performative optima rather than stable fixed points
subfield: Robustness, domain shift, and performative effects
open: Can we learn a globally good performative decision when deploying the predictor itself shifts the data distribution, without confusing distributional stability with optimality? Formally, the goal is to optimize the performative risk over the family of distributions induced by the deployed model, rather than merely converging to a stable fixed point of the response dynamics.
status: Performative prediction has supplied convergence results under structural conditions since 2020, notably in Perdomo, Zrnic, Mendler-Dünner, and Hardt (2020), *Performative Prediction*, arXiv:2002.06673. General global optimization under unknown response dynamics remains a target.
solved_when: An algorithm is given that, under unknown response dynamics, finds a decision whose performative risk is globally near-optimal — not merely stable — with guarantees on the quality of the solution.
why: A system can stabilize at a self-confirming but socially or operationally poor outcome; solving this ensures convergence reflects genuine optimality rather than a trap created by the model's own influence on the data.
key_works: Perdomo, Zrnic, Mendler-Dünner, and Hardt (2020), *Performative Prediction*, arXiv:2002.06673.

title: Multi-agent performative learning
subfield: Robustness, domain shift, and performative effects
open: Characterize convergence, welfare, and learnability when several independently adapting predictors jointly change the population they observe — a formal account of what stability and optimality mean when each learner's data distribution is shifted by the others' deployed models.
status: Research target. Single-deployer stability assumptions do not generally survive interacting strategic learners. Key works: Perdomo et al. (2020), arXiv:2002.06673; Foster et al. (2023), *On the Complexity of Multi-Agent Decision Making*, arXiv:2305.00684.
solved_when: A framework exists that gives checkable conditions under which interacting performative learners converge, together with guarantees on welfare and learnability that provably extend single-deployer results to the multi-agent setting.
why: Markets, recommendation ecosystems, and competing platforms contain multiple adaptive decision-makers, so single-deployer theory does not cover the deployed reality.
key_works: Perdomo et al. (2020), arXiv:2002.06673; Foster et al. (2023), *On the Complexity of Multi-Agent Decision Making*, arXiv:2305.00684.

title: Sharp conditional coverage under explicit regularity
open: Under a stated smoothness or low-complexity conditional model, determine the optimal tradeoff between local coverage accuracy and prediction-set size.
status: Exact nontrivial distribution-free conditional coverage is already impossible, as shown by Barber, Candès, Ramdas, and Tibshirani (2020), *The Limits of Distribution-Free Conditional Predictive Inference*, arXiv:1903.04684; the open target is a sharp restricted-model frontier.
solved_when: A sharp frontier is established for the restricted model class: matching (up to constants) upper and lower bounds on the achievable tradeoff between local conditional coverage accuracy and prediction-set size.
why: Marginal coverage can conceal severe errors for particular inputs or populations, so a sharp restricted-model frontier is what makes conditional guarantees trustworthy and usable.
key_works: Barber, Candès, Ramdas, and Tibshirani (2020), *The Limits of Distribution-Free Conditional Predictive Inference*, arXiv:1903.04684.

title: Finite-window adaptive coverage with efficient sets
open: Can a single online prediction procedure guarantee valid coverage on every short window of a deployment while keeping prediction sets small, when distribution drift is bounded by an explicit budget? A complete answer should quantify the trade-off between window length, drift budget, and set size, and be backed by matching lower bounds.
status: Long-run adaptive coverage methods exist, but long-run average validity alone does not guarantee useful coverage during a particular deployment interval. Key works: Gibbs and Candès (2021), *Adaptive Conformal Inference Under Distribution Shift*, arXiv:2106.00170; Barber et al. (2023), *Conformal Prediction Beyond Exchangeability*, arXiv:2202.13415.
solved_when: An algorithm is given that simultaneously controls window-wise miscoverage and prediction-set size under a stated drift budget, together with lower bounds showing the achieved trade-off is tight.
why: Long-run averages let a prediction system compensate for a dangerous failure period with later overcoverage, so practitioners currently have no guarantee of useful coverage during the interval that actually matters.
key_works: Gibbs and Candès (2021), *Adaptive Conformal Inference Under Distribution Shift*, arXiv:2106.00170; Barber et al. (2023), *Conformal Prediction Beyond Exchangeability*, arXiv:2202.13415.

bib.title: Finite-window adaptive coverage with efficient sets

title: Risk control for variable-length generated outputs
open: Can we build conformal-style sets or abstention policies for generated outputs of unbounded length that provably control a semantic loss — even when the loss itself is only measured by an uncertain evaluator?
status: This is currently an open research target. Conformal risk control (Angelopoulos et al. (2024), *Conformal Risk Control*, arXiv:2208.02814) provides a general framework, but semantic evaluation of generated text and the enormous size of the output space introduce unresolved requirements the framework does not address.
solved_when: A construction exists that outputs practically sized sets or abstention rules for variable-length generated outputs with a distribution-free guarantee on the chosen semantic loss, accounting for evaluator uncertainty.
why: It would carry uncertainty guarantees beyond fixed-label classification into the regime where modern generative models actually operate, where semantic errors and huge output spaces defeat existing tools.
key_works: Angelopoulos et al. (2024), *Conformal Risk Control*, arXiv:2208.02814.

title: Unknown-dependence conformal prediction
open: Can we construct prediction intervals for sequentially observed data whose temporal dependence structure is unknown and possibly changing, so that finite-sample coverage guarantees are preserved while interval widths stay reasonably sharp? Formally, the goal is a distribution-free procedure whose validity degrades gracefully with the (unknown, time-varying) dependence strength rather than only with departures from exchangeability.
status: Current beyond-exchangeability methods, notably Barber et al. (2023), *Conformal Prediction Beyond Exchangeability*, arXiv:2202.13415, quantify how coverage degrades under departures from the ideal exchangeability assumption, and related tools such as Howard et al. (2021), *Time-Uniform, Nonparametric, Nonasymptotic Confidence Sequences*, arXiv:1810.08240, provide time-uniform nonparametric inference; however, adapting to the strength of unknown dependence itself remains a separate, unachieved target.
solved_when: A procedure exists that, under unknown temporal dependence, maintains finite-sample validity guarantees and achieves interval widths that are not excessively conservative — i.e., the widths adapt to the actual dependence strength instead of assuming a worst case.
why: Sequential observations in practice often carry dependence that changes over time, so conformal methods that assume exchangeability either lose validity or must over-widen to compensate; an adaptive solution would make distribution-free uncertainty quantification usable directly on realistic time series.
key_works: Barber et al. (2023), *Conformal Prediction Beyond Exchangeability*, arXiv:2202.13415; Howard et al. (2021), *Time-Uniform, Nonparametric, Nonasymptotic Confidence Sequences*, arXiv:1810.08240.

title: Selective uncertainty after adaptive model comparison
open: Can prediction-set and risk guarantees from conformal-type methods survive when users adaptively compare, filter, and select among models or prediction sets on the basis of the same calibration data? Formally, under what selection rules or correction mechanisms does the coverage or risk bound of a prespecified conformal procedure remain valid after such adaptive selection?
status: This is an open research target. It is known that the validity of one prespecified conformal procedure does not automatically survive unrestricted adaptive selection. Related literature includes Dwork et al. (2015), arXiv:1506.02629, and Angelopoulos et al. (2024), *Conformal Risk Control*, arXiv:2208.02814; the problem also connects to selective inference in statistics and reusable calibration in adaptive data analysis.
solved_when: A procedure is given that provably preserves the calibration-based guarantee (e.g., coverage or risk control at the nominal level) under a specified class of adaptive comparisons and selections using the same calibration information, with the guarantee stated and proved.
why: Deployment workflows routinely pick the narrowest-looking or best-performing uncertainty method after inspecting results, so guarantees that silently fail under this common practice are of little use in practice.
key_works: Dwork et al. (2015), arXiv:1506.02629; Angelopoulos et al. (2024), *Conformal Risk Control*, arXiv:2208.02814.

title: Uncertainty decomposition that is empirically identifiable
open: When can we actually tell apart the different sources of a model's predictive uncertainty? Formally, under a specified model family and a repeated-data protocol, determine which components of predictive uncertainty can be separated into irreducible noise, finite-data uncertainty, and model misspecification.
status: This is a proposed target. No method exists; naming uncertainty components does not establish that they are identifiable from one trained model's outputs. Related threads appear in conformal prediction (Barber et al. (2020), arXiv:1903.04684), widely applicable Bayesian information criteria (Watanabe (2013), *A Widely Applicable Bayesian Information Criterion*), identifiability of variance components in measurement theory, and model discrepancy in inverse problems.
solved_when: A protocol is given that, from a trained model's outputs under the specified model family and repeated-data protocol, recovers a decomposition of predictive uncertainty into irreducible noise, finite-data uncertainty, and model misspecification, with empirical evidence that the components are identifiable.
why: Different uncertainty sources call for different interventions — collecting more data, choosing a different model, or accepting irreducible ambiguity — so a trustworthy decomposition tells practitioners which remedy actually applies.
key_works: Barber et al. (2020), arXiv:1903.04684; Watanabe (2013), *A Widely Applicable Bayesian Information Criterion*.

title: How much harder is approximately private PAC learning?
open: Does approximately differentially private PAC learning of finite concept classes ever require substantially more samples than the nonprivate VC-dimension bound suggests, beyond the separations currently known? In other words, is the quantitative sample-complexity gap between approximate-DP and nonprivate learning of finite classes large or essentially bounded?
status: Raised as an explicit open question at COLT 2026 and posed by Nissim, Stemmer, and Tsfadia (2026), *Invited Open Problem: Does Differential Privacy Make PAC Learning Much Harder?* Approximate-DP learnability and online learnability are known to coincide qualitatively, but this qualitative equivalence does not settle the quantitative gap for finite classes.
solved_when: A determination, in either direction, of whether approximately differentially private learners for finite concept classes can have sample complexity exceeding the nonprivate VC-based bound by a large factor, going beyond presently understood separations.
why: It settles whether privacy's worst-case statistical price in PAC learning is fundamentally modest or very large — a basic question about the cost of privacy in machine learning.
key_works: Nissim, Stemmer, and Tsfadia (2026), *Invited Open Problem: Does Differential Privacy Make PAC Learning Much Harder?*

bib.title: How much harder is approximately private PAC learning?

title: Computationally useful private learning under distributional restrictions
open: Can the recent characterizations of which concept classes are privately learnable under distributional restrictions be converted into algorithms that are actually efficient, with sample complexity and runtime depending sharply on the restriction parameters? In other words, does the qualitative learnability theory for these restricted settings carry a quantitative, computationally useful counterpart?
status: Qualitative characterizations of online and private learnability under distributional constraints via generalized smoothness appeared in 2026, in Blanchard, Shetty, and Rakhlin (2026), *Characterizing Online and Private Learnability under Distributional Constraints via Generalized Smoothness*. However, a characterization of learnability is not the same as an efficient implementation for an implicit class, so the computational question remains open.
solved_when: An efficient learning algorithm is given whose sample complexity and runtime are controlled explicitly by the parameters of the distributional restriction (e.g., the generalized-smoothness parameters), with sharp dependence on those parameters, for an implicitly specified class.
why: Real datasets often satisfy structural assumptions that worst-case private-learning theory ignores; exploiting them could make privacy far cheaper—less data and less compute—than general theory predicts.
key_works: Blanchard, Shetty, and Rakhlin (2026), *Characterizing Online and Private Learnability under Distributional Constraints via Generalized Smoothness*.

title: Optimal deletion-capacity tradeoffs
open: How much accuracy, memory, and update time must a learning system sacrifice to support a long sequence of adaptive deletion requests? More formally, determine matching upper and lower bounds for the accuracy–memory–update-time–deletion-capacity tradeoff frontier in repeated machine unlearning under adaptively chosen deletions.
status: Currently a research target. Existing unlearning theory provides important tradeoffs, but the full adaptive resource frontier remains undetermined, as it depends on training and storage constraints. Key works: Sekhari et al. (2021), *Remember What You Want to Forget: Algorithms for Machine Unlearning*, arXiv:2103.03279; Neel et al. (2021), arXiv:2007.02923.
solved_when: Matching upper and lower bounds are established for accuracy, memory, update time, and deletion capacity under adaptive deletion requests, across the relevant training and storage constraints.
why: Handling a single deletion is fundamentally different from economically supporting many successive deletions; tight tradeoffs would tell us which unlearning systems can scale to realistic deletion workloads and which cannot.
key_works: Sekhari et al. (2021), *Remember What You Want to Forget: Algorithms for Machine Unlearning*, arXiv:2103.03279; Neel et al. (2021), arXiv:2007.02923.

bib.title: Optimal deletion-capacity tradeoffs

title: Unlearning through derived models and artifacts
open: When a model's data is deleted, what guarantee can be made that the deletion propagates to everything derived from it — finetuned descendants, distilled models, cached embeddings, and other downstream artifacts? The goal is to define deletion guarantees over the full derived-model dependency graph and design mechanisms that enforce them.
status: Proposed target; no solution is known. Foundational unlearning results exist — Bourtoule et al. (2021), *Machine Unlearning*, arXiv:1912.03817, and Sekhari et al. (2021), arXiv:2103.03279 — but a guarantee for one model state does not automatically remove information from its descendants. Related ideas appear in provenance-aware deletion in databases and transitive noninterference in information-flow security.
solved_when: A formal notion of deletion covering derived models and artifacts exists, together with an enforcement mechanism that verifiably removes the influence of deleted data from a model and all of its finetuned descendants, distilled models, cached embeddings, and other derivatives.
why: Modern training systems form dependency graphs rather than isolated model files, so a deletion guarantee for one model state does not automatically remove information from its descendants.
key_works: Bourtoule et al. (2021), *Machine Unlearning*, arXiv:1912.03817; Sekhari et al. (2021), arXiv:2103.03279.

title: Private learning with rare, changing user groups
open: Can a learner guarantee meaningful user-level differential privacy and good worst-group accuracy even when participation rates and group prevalence shift over time, with sharp dependence on the smallest supported groups? More precisely, the goal is a construction whose privacy and accuracy guarantees degrade gracefully under heterogeneous, changing participation while remaining sensitive to the size of the rarest groups.
status: This is an open research target combining privacy, heterogeneous participation, and group-robust learning; no construction is known. Related context comes from Kairouz et al. (2021), *Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning*, arXiv:1912.04977, and Sagawa et al. (2020), arXiv:1911.08731, with connections to survey statistics on rare strata and privacy-theoretic user-level composition.
solved_when: A learning procedure is constructed that simultaneously achieves user-level differential privacy and nontrivial worst-group accuracy under changing participation rates and group prevalence, with sharp (quantitatively characterized) dependence on the smallest supported groups.
why: Average privacy-preserving accuracy can conceal failure for infrequent users or small populations; a solution would ensure such users and groups are protected and well-served rather than hidden in the aggregate.
key_works: Kairouz et al. (2021), *Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning*, arXiv:1912.04977; Sagawa et al. (2020), arXiv:1911.08731.

title: Numerically faithful privacy guarantees
open: Can we build a full pipeline in which the privacy guarantee that is proven on paper is provably the one delivered by the running code? Concretely, this means an end-to-end accounting and implementation framework showing that finite-precision randomness, clipping, aggregation, and adaptive training together preserve the claimed privacy parameters.
status: This is a proposed infrastructure target; currently, mathematical privacy analysis and concrete numerical implementation exist as separate objects requiring a verified connection. Kairouz et al. (2021), *Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning*, arXiv:1912.04977.
solved_when: A verified framework connects the mathematical privacy analysis to a concrete numerical implementation, covering finite-precision randomness, clipping, aggregation, and adaptive training, with the implemented mechanism provably preserving the claimed privacy parameters.
why: A privacy theorem is not sufficient when the implemented random mechanism differs from the analyzed one; without a verified connection, deployed systems may deliver weaker privacy than their guarantees state.
key_works: Kairouz et al. (2021), *Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning*, arXiv:1912.04977.

title: Joint privacy–unlearning optimality
open: When does training with differential privacy optimally reduce the cost of later machine unlearning requests, and when does stronger privacy merely sacrifice accuracy without yielding any meaningful unlearning benefit?
status: An open research target. It is known that differential privacy and unlearning are related but impose different operational requirements. Relevant work includes Sekhari et al. (2021), *Remember What You Want to Forget*, arXiv:2103.03279, and Nissim et al. (2026), *Does Differential Privacy Make PAC Learning Much Harder?*
solved_when: A characterization is given of the regimes in which adding privacy during training reduces future deletion cost optimally, together with the regimes in which stronger privacy provides no meaningful unlearning benefit beyond its accuracy cost.
why: It tells practitioners when it is worth paying an upfront privacy cost during training versus maintaining expensive dedicated deletion infrastructure.
key_works: Sekhari et al. (2021), *Remember What You Want to Forget*, arXiv:2103.03279; Nissim et al. (2026), *Does Differential Privacy Make PAC Learning Much Harder?*

title: Sharp conversions between privacy, stability, and replicability
open: When a learner is converted from satisfying one of privacy, stability, or replicability to another, how much must one pay in sample complexity and accuracy for specific problem families? A sharp answer would pin down the optimal parameter losses of these conversions rather than just their existence.
status: Research target. Connections among the notions exist, but the properties are not interchangeable at identical sample and computational cost; no sharp conversions are known. Key works: Impagliazzo et al. (2022), *Reproducibility in Learning*, arXiv:2201.08430; Nissim et al. (2026), *Does Differential Privacy Make PAC Learning Much Harder?*
solved_when: For explicit problem families, matching upper and lower bounds are established on the parameter (sample and computational cost) losses of conversions among private, stable, and replicable learners.
why: It would reveal whether a single training mechanism can deliver several reliability guarantees efficiently, or whether the properties are inherently non-interchangeable at identical cost.
key_works: Impagliazzo et al. (2022), *Reproducibility in Learning*, arXiv:2201.08430; Nissim et al. (2026), *Does Differential Privacy Make PAC Learning Much Harder?*

title: Replicability under adaptive composition
open: Can an entire adaptively chosen sequence of learning and decision steps be made replicable, so that repeating the whole workflow on fresh samples of the data yields the same sequence of decisions with high probability? Formally, this asks for a replication guarantee for a composed pipeline, not merely for one isolated estimator.
status: This is currently a research target; no compositional guarantee is known, and the central difficulty is that errors and data dependence can compound when replicated components are assembled into a workflow. Key works: Impagliazzo et al. (2022), arXiv:2201.08430; Dwork et al. (2015), arXiv:1506.02629.
solved_when: A construction (or proof) exists that guarantees replication of the full adaptively composed workflow, with error controlled under composition rather than compounding as components are assembled.
why: Scientific and industrial pipelines make many contingent decisions after inspecting intermediate results, and errors and data dependence can compound when replicated components are assembled into a workflow; without composition, replicability theory does not apply to how these pipelines are actually run.
key_works: Impagliazzo et al. (2022), arXiv:2201.08430; Dwork et al. (2015), arXiv:1506.02629.

title: Reusable evaluation under a changing population
open: Can we guarantee valid, adaptive evaluation error control for a benchmark that is queried repeatedly while the population it is meant to represent is itself drifting over time? In other words, can reusable-holdout guarantees be extended to a setting where the deployment distribution changes between queries?
status: Research target. Reusable-holdout methods address adaptivity (Dwork et al. (2015), *Generalization in Adaptive Data Analysis and Holdout Reuse*, arXiv:1506.02629), and distribution-shift methods address drift (Barber et al. (2023), arXiv:2202.13415); their joint sharp treatment remains open and requires combining both.
solved_when: A framework is given that jointly handles adaptivity from repeated benchmark queries and distribution shift in the underlying population, with provable error control for evaluations under both effects simultaneously.
why: A benchmark can remain statistically protected against overuse yet become irrelevant to current deployment; without a joint treatment, validity guarantees and relevance to real-world use drift apart.
key_works: Dwork et al. (2015), *Generalization in Adaptive Data Analysis and Holdout Reuse*, arXiv:1506.02629; Barber et al. (2023), arXiv:2202.13415.

title: Counterexample generation for theorem assumptions
open: Build a system that, given a learning theorem's formal assumptions, automatically generates small counterexamples when a claimed application violates a necessary condition. In effect: a standardized assumption-to-counterexample workflow for machine learning theory.
status: Proposed infrastructure target. Existing theory supplies many isolated impossibility constructions, but not a standardized assumption-to-counterexample workflow. Key works: Goel et al. (2026), *Testing Noise Assumptions of Learning Algorithms*; Nagarajan and Kolter (2019), arXiv:1902.04742. Related areas include formal verification—counterexample-guided abstraction refinement—and automated reasoning—model finding.
solved_when: A working system exists that takes a theorem's formal assumptions as input and outputs small counterexamples for applications violating a necessary condition.
why: It would reduce misapplication of theorems to incompatible data, access models, or computational regimes.
key_works: Goel et al. (2026), *Testing Noise Assumptions of Learning Algorithms*; Nagarajan and Kolter (2019), arXiv:1902.04742.

title: Machine-checkable learning-theory benchmark claims
open: Can we design a benchmark format in which the assumptions of a learning-theory theorem, the exact algorithm version tested, the numerical experiments, and any claimed rate comparisons can all be independently replayed and machine-checked by a third party?
status: Currently a proposed infrastructure target; no claim is made that existing theorem provers or reproducibility initiatives are absent. Related efforts include Impagliazzo et al. (2022), *Reproducibility in Learning*, arXiv:2201.08430, and Berner et al. (2021), *The Modern Mathematics of Deep Learning*, arXiv:2105.04026; adjacent areas are proof libraries in formal mathematics and reproducible builds in software engineering.
solved_when: A working format and toolchain exist under which theorem assumptions, algorithm versions, numerical experiments, and claimed rate comparisons can each be independently replayed and verified.
why: It would expose mismatches between asymptotic claims, the algorithms actually implemented, and the empirical evidence reported, making benchmark-based theory claims falsifiable.
key_works: Impagliazzo et al. (2022), *Reproducibility in Learning*, arXiv:2201.08430; Berner et al. (2021), *The Modern Mathematics of Deep Learning*, arXiv:2105.04026.

title: Is interaction necessary for optimal one-bit mean estimation?
open: Can arbitrary nonadaptive one-bit quantizers attain order-optimal mean-estimation rates over the specified finite-moment distribution classes, or is interaction necessary?
status: This is posed as an explicit COLT 2026 problem. Adaptive and two-stage protocols are known to attain the optimal rates, while nonadaptive threshold and interval schemes can be suboptimal; the key reference is Lau and Scarlett (2026), *Open Problem: Is Interaction Necessary for Order-Optimal 1-bit Mean Estimation?*
solved_when: Either a nonadaptive one-bit quantizer is shown to attain the order-optimal mean-estimation rate over the specified finite-moment distribution classes, matching the adaptive and two-stage protocols, or a lower bound is proved showing every nonadaptive scheme is strictly suboptimal relative to interactive ones.
why: It isolates the statistical value of feedback when each observation contributes only one bit, determining whether adaptivity is a genuine resource or merely a proof convenience in communication-constrained estimation.
key_works: Lau and Scarlett (2026), *Open Problem: Is Interaction Necessary for Order-Optimal 1-bit Mean Estimation?*

title: Learning under informative client availability
open: When clients in federated learning participate in ways that depend on their private data or on the current model's behavior, how can we detect and correct the resulting participation bias? The goal is to characterize when such missing-not-at-random participation is identifiable and to build learning procedures that correct for it under explicit identifiability assumptions.
status: This is an open research target. Standard heterogeneous-data analyses in federated learning do not automatically cover missing-not-at-random participation, and no existing framework supplies the needed correction. Key works: Kairouz et al. (2021), *Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning*, arXiv:1912.04977; McMahan et al. (2017), *Communication-Efficient Learning of Deep Networks from Decentralized Data*, arXiv:1602.05629.
solved_when: A method exists that provably identifies and corrects participation bias arising from data- or model-dependent client availability, with guarantees stated under explicit identifiability assumptions.
why: A federated model can systematically underlearn from users who rarely participate, so without such a correction the trained model is skewed toward frequently available clients no matter how good the aggregation scheme is.
key_works: Kairouz et al. (2021), *Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning*, arXiv:1912.04977; McMahan et al. (2017), *Communication-Efficient Learning of Deep Networks from Decentralized Data*, arXiv:1602.05629.

title: Instance-optimal federated personalization
open: Can a federated learning system attain the best possible tradeoff between shared and client-specific estimation without knowing in advance how heterogeneous the clients are or how that heterogeneity is structured? In other words, is there a universal personalization rule whose performance matches the instance-optimal choice on every problem?
status: This remains a research target. Existing heterogeneity-correction methods, such as Karimireddy et al. (2020), *SCAFFOLD: Stochastic Controlled Averaging for Federated Learning*, arXiv:1910.06378, provide important guarantees, but no universal instance-optimal personalization rule is known; the field is surveyed in Kairouz et al. (2021), arXiv:1912.04977.
solved_when: A single personalization procedure is shown to achieve the instance-optimal sharing–personalization tradeoff for every instance, with no prior knowledge of the degree or structure of client heterogeneity.
why: Excessive sharing harms unusual clients, while excessive personalization wastes common information; an instance-optimal rule would let each federation extract the full value of both without tuning to assumptions that may not hold.
key_works: Karimireddy et al. (2020), *SCAFFOLD: Stochastic Controlled Averaging for Federated Learning*, arXiv:1910.06378; Kairouz et al. (2021), arXiv:1912.04977.

title: Privacy, secure aggregation, and Byzantine robustness together
open: Can federated learning simultaneously deliver accuracy, Byzantine robustness, and user-level privacy when the server observes only secure aggregates of client updates? Formally, determine sharp accuracy and breakdown guarantees in a setting where some clients are malicious and honest clients require user-level privacy.
status: This is an open research target. Guarantees proved with individually inspectable updates do not automatically survive secure aggregation. Key works: Kairouz et al. (2021), *Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning*, arXiv:1912.04977.
solved_when: Provable accuracy and breakdown guarantees are established for learning under secure aggregation, malicious clients, and user-level privacy, matching the sharp rates achievable when these constraints are absent.
why: Privacy mechanisms can destroy exactly the information a robust aggregator needs, so without such guarantees robustness and privacy cannot be safely combined in federated learning.
key_works: Kairouz et al. (2021), *Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning*, arXiv:1912.04977.

title: Total-bit complexity of heterogeneous stochastic optimization
open: Can we characterize the total cost of solving a distributed stochastic optimization problem with heterogeneous client objectives when every resource is counted — all transmitted bits, communication rounds, local computation, and final statistical error? In other words, what are matching upper and lower bounds on this joint bit-round-computation-error complexity measure?
status: This is currently a research target; no such joint bounds are known. Related lines of work include McMahan et al. (2017), arXiv:1602.05629; Karimireddy et al. (2020), *SCAFFOLD*, arXiv:1910.06378, along with communication-complexity lower bounds for distributed optimization and gradient-quantization methods from coding theory.
solved_when: Matching upper and lower bounds are established for a heterogeneous-client stochastic optimization setting, accounting simultaneously for transmitted bits, communication rounds, local computation, and the final statistical error.
why: It would make communication-efficiency claims comparable across distributed algorithms, since round complexity alone can hide large messages or excessive local work.
key_works: McMahan et al. (2017), arXiv:1602.05629; Karimireddy et al. (2020), *SCAFFOLD*, arXiv:1910.06378.

bib.title: Total-bit complexity of heterogeneous stochastic optimization

title: Adaptive communication without oracle heterogeneity parameters
open: Can a distributed learning algorithm choose its communication schedule — how many local updates to take, when to synchronize, and how coarsely to quantize — online, while matching the performance of the best fixed policy chosen in hindsight with full knowledge of the clients' data heterogeneity? In other words, can adaptivity in communication compensate for the heterogeneity parameters that static tuning assumes are known?
status: This remains a research target; no solution is recorded. Existing key works address communication-efficient and heterogeneous distributed learning but rely on fixed tuning: Karimireddy et al. (2020), *SCAFFOLD*, arXiv:1910.06378, and McMahan et al. (2017), arXiv:1602.05629. Related directions include online algorithms for adaptive resource allocation and event-triggered synchronization from control theory.
solved_when: An online algorithm selecting local-update counts, synchronization frequency, and quantization levels is shown to match the best fixed policy chosen with knowledge of the data heterogeneity, without requiring those heterogeneity parameters as oracle inputs.
why: It would reduce communication in distributed learning without causing uncontrolled client drift, removing the circularity where static tuning demands the very heterogeneity information that the learning process is itself trying to discover.
key_works: Karimireddy et al. (2020), *SCAFFOLD*, arXiv:1910.06378; McMahan et al. (2017), arXiv:1602.05629.

title: Task-aware limits of oversquashing repair
open: What is the minimum amount of architectural change or graph rewiring needed to preserve the information a given long-range graph task actually depends on? Formally, characterize the task-aware resource requirement — in terms of connectivity modification or architectural capacity — for alleviating oversquashing while retaining task-relevant graph semantics.
status: Oversquashing and message-passing bottlenecks are established phenomena, as in Alon and Yahav (2021), *On the Bottleneck of Graph Neural Networks and Its Practical Implications*, arXiv:2006.05205; however, existing universal rewiring heuristics fall short of a task-specific optimality theorem. Related tools come from graph theory (expansion and separators) and communication complexity (distributed information bottlenecks).
solved_when: A theorem (or matching bounds) identifies the minimum architectural or graph-rewiring resources sufficient to preserve task-relevant information for a specified long-range graph task, separating necessary rewiring from modifications that needlessly alter graph semantics.
why: It would separate useful connectivity changes from expensive modifications that destroy relevant graph semantics, giving principled guidance where current rewiring heuristics are applied blindly.
key_works: Alon and Yahav (2021), *On the Bottleneck of Graph Neural Networks and Its Practical Implications*, arXiv:2006.05205.

bib.title: Task-aware limits of oversquashing repair

title: Statistical efficiency of higher-order graph expressivity
open: When does increasing a graph network's expressivity beyond ordinary message passing actually pay off? That is, quantify the conditions under which higher-order expressivity improves learnable risk enough to justify its sample and computational cost.
status: Expressivity hierarchies are well developed, but representational distinctions alone do not settle statistical or optimization benefits. Key works: Xu, Hu, Leskovec, and Jegelka (2019), *How Powerful are Graph Neural Networks?*, arXiv:1810.00826. Related connections include finite model theory (Weisfeiler–Leman hierarchies) and graph isomorphism (resource-bounded distinguishability).
solved_when: A characterization is given — as theory, e.g., bounds or trade-off results — of when the gain in learnable risk from moving beyond ordinary message passing exceeds the added sample and computational cost.
why: More expressive graph models can be substantially more expensive without improving the task, so practitioners currently have no principled basis for choosing their level of expressivity.
key_works: Xu, Hu, Leskovec, and Jegelka (2019), *How Powerful Are Graph Neural Networks?*, arXiv:1810.00826.

bib.title: Statistical efficiency of higher-order graph expressivity

title: Provable optimization for graph algorithm extrapolation
open: Can gradient-based training actually find the structured solutions that algorithmic graph extrapolation depends on, rather than merely assuming the regularized objective has been minimized? Formally, prove that practical optimization reaches the minima at which the known representation-and-generalization guarantees hold.
status: A 2026 shortest-path result by Nerem, Chen, Dasgupta, and Wang, *Graph Neural Networks Extrapolate Out-of-Distribution for Shortest Paths*, proves that suitably minimized sparse objectives implement Bellman–Ford steps; optimization of those objectives is a distinct, open requirement.
solved_when: A proof (under an explicit training model) that optimizing the regularized objective reaches the sparse, structured solutions implementing the algorithmic steps — establishing the optimization premise of the extrapolation guarantee as a training guarantee rather than an assumption.
why: Without it, the representation-and-generalization theorem rests on an unverified premise: no guarantee that trained models actually attain the structured minima that make out-of-distribution algorithmic extrapolation work.
key_works: Nerem, Chen, Dasgupta, and Wang (2026), *Graph Neural Networks Extrapolate Out-of-Distribution for Shortest Paths*.

title: Size extrapolation for graph algorithms beyond shortest paths
open: Can we build a trainable architecture with certified size extrapolation for a precisely specified graph algorithm other than shortest paths, including a characterization of its approximation or computational limits?
status: This is a research target following the 2026 shortest-path result of Nerem et al. (2026), *Graph Neural Networks Extrapolate Out-of-Distribution for Shortest Paths*; that theorem does not cover arbitrary graph algorithms. Related foundations trace to Xu et al. (2019), arXiv:1810.00826.
solved_when: A neural architecture is shown, with proof, to extrapolate out-of-distribution in graph size for some precisely specified graph algorithm beyond shortest paths, together with a treatment of the algorithm's approximation or computational limits.
why: It would reveal whether neural algorithmic alignment generalizes beyond especially favorable dynamic programs, rather than being an artifact of the shortest-path setting.
key_works: Nerem et al. (2026), *Graph Neural Networks Extrapolate Out-of-Distribution for Shortest Paths*; Xu et al. (2019), arXiv:1810.00826.

title: Unknown continuous symmetry discovery
open: Can we learn a continuous symmetry group directly from data when the group itself is unknown, rather than only detecting invariance to a group specified in advance? The goal is a method with computational and statistical guarantees that extend beyond the finite-group subgroup-lattice setting.
status: Known-group invariance, including for infinite groups, has polynomial-time results from Soleymani et al. (2026), *Efficient Learning and Symmetry Discovery under Exact Invariances*, which also addresses discovery of unknown finite groups; unknown continuous-group discovery remains a different, open target.
solved_when: An algorithm discovers an unknown continuous symmetry group from data and comes with provable computational and statistical guarantees.
why: Scientific data often contain unknown rotations, scalings, or continuous conservation symmetries, so recovering them automatically would reveal structure that is currently assumed or missed.
key_works: Soleymani et al. (2026), *Efficient Learning and Symmetry Discovery under Exact Invariances*.

title: End-to-end mesh-independent operator learning
subfield: Scientific machine learning and operator learning
open: Can we prove an end-to-end learning guarantee for operator learning whose error and computational cost stay controlled when the evaluation resolution changes? That is, a theorem tying training, approximation, and deployment together so that refining the mesh neither silently degrades accuracy nor blows up the computational accounting.
status: Neural-operator approximation frameworks exist, but discretization-invariant architecture alone does not constitute an end-to-end mesh-independent learning theorem. Key works: Kovachki et al. (2023), *Neural Operator: Learning Maps Between Function Spaces*, arXiv:2108.08481; Lu et al. (2019 preprint), *DeepONet*, arXiv:1910.03193.
solved_when: A complete training-to-deployment guarantee is established whose error and computational accounting remain controlled under changes in evaluation resolution.
why: Scientific models should not silently fail when a simulation grid is refined; such a theorem would make operator networks trustworthy tools for numerical simulation rather than architecture-level promises.
key_works: Kovachki et al. (2023), *Neural Operator: Learning Maps Between Function Spaces*, arXiv:2108.08481; Lu et al. (2019 preprint), *DeepONet*, arXiv:1910.03193.

title: Long-horizon statistical accuracy for learned chaotic dynamics
subfield: Scientific machine learning and operator learning
open: Can we prove that a learned model of a chaotic dynamical system reproduces the system's long-run statistics — its invariant measure or long-time averages of observables — without requiring the impossible standard of indefinite pointwise trajectory agreement?
status: This remains an open research target. What is known is negative in spirit: short-horizon prediction error does not automatically control long-run statistical behavior. Key works in operator learning include Kovachki et al. (2023), *Neural Operator*, arXiv:2108.08481, and Lu et al., *DeepONet*, arXiv:1910.03193; related mathematical machinery includes statistical stability in dynamical systems and shadowing and invariant measures in numerical analysis.
solved_when: A guarantee is established that bounds the error of the learned model's invariant measure (or long-time observable statistics) for chaotic systems, quantifying the trade-off between training/prediction error and long-horizon statistical accuracy rather than demanding exact trajectory matching.
why: Climate, fluid, and many-body applications often care about long-term statistics rather than exact trajectories, so a proof of statistical fidelity would certify learned simulators for exactly the uses they are intended for.
key_works: Kovachki et al. (2023), *Neural Operator*, arXiv:2108.08481; Lu et al., *DeepONet*, arXiv:1910.03193.

title: Certified global residual control from sampled physics constraints
subfield: Scientific machine learning and operator learning
open: Can a finite set of sampled residual evaluations be turned into a rigorous certificate that the true solution error is small everywhere, for a specified PDE class and neural approximation family?
status: Proposed target. It is known that small residuals at collocation points do not alone certify small error over the entire domain. Background includes Berner et al. (2021), *The Modern Mathematics of Deep Learning*, arXiv:2105.04026, and Kovachki et al. (2023), *Neural Operator*, arXiv:2108.08481.
solved_when: A method exists that, from finitely many residual checks, produces a guaranteed global bound on solution error over the entire domain, valid for the stated PDE class and approximation family.
why: It would make physics-constrained learning auditable for scientific use, replacing pointwise optimism with trustworthy error guarantees.
key_works: Berner et al. (2021), *The Modern Mathematics of Deep Learning*, arXiv:2105.04026; Kovachki et al. (2023), *Neural Operator*, arXiv:2108.08481.

title: Instance-optimal shadow tomography outside the high-precision regime
open: Can shadow tomography of an unknown quantum state achieve instance-optimal sample complexity in the moderate-accuracy regime, beyond the high-precision thresholds where local metrological analysis applies? Formally, the goal is to extend sharp instance-dependent few-copy guarantees to accuracies outside the regime covered by local Fisher-information analysis.
status: A 2026 result characterizes high-precision sample complexity through inverse Fisher information, up to logarithmic factors: Chen, Gong, and Zhou (2026), *Instance-Optimal High-Precision Shadow Tomography with Few-Copy Measurements: A Metrological Approach*.
solved_when: Instance-dependent sample-complexity bounds for shadow tomography with few-copy measurements are established, up to logarithmic factors, for accuracy parameters lying beyond the high-precision thresholds required by local metrological analysis.
why: It would cover the moderate-accuracy regime relevant to many experiments, which the current high-precision theory does not reach.
key_works: Chen, Gong, and Zhou (2026), *Instance-Optimal High-Precision Shadow Tomography with Few-Copy Measurements: A Metrological Approach*.

title: End-to-end quantum learning advantage on natural data
open: Can a quantum learner demonstrate a genuine, reproducible advantage on a naturally motivated learning task once all costs are charged honestly? That is, after accounting for data access, state preparation, measurement, classical preprocessing, and error correction in the end-to-end pipeline.
status: Rigorous supervised quantum separations exist, but they do not automatically establish practical end-to-end advantage under realistic access costs. Key works: Liu, Arunachalam, and Temme (2021), *A Rigorous and Robust Quantum Speed-up in Supervised Machine Learning*, arXiv:2010.02174; Huang et al. (2021), *Power of Data in Quantum Machine Learning*, arXiv:2011.01938.
solved_when: A reproducible learning advantage is demonstrated on a naturally motivated task in a full end-to-end accounting that includes data access, state preparation, measurement, classical preprocessing, and error correction.
why: It would distinguish genuine algorithmic speedup from merely moving costs into the input model, which is where current separations fall short of practical claims.
key_works: Liu, Arunachalam, and Temme (2021), *A Rigorous and Robust Quantum Speed-up in Supervised Machine Learning*, arXiv:2010.02174; Huang et al. (2021), *Power of Data in Quantum Machine Learning*, arXiv:2011.01938.

title: Expressive, trainable, noise-tolerant quantum models
open: Can one construct a family of trainable quantum models that is simultaneously expressive enough to be classically hard to simulate, free of barren plateaus, and robust to realistic noise? Formally, the goal is a quantum-model family that avoids barren plateaus, retains meaningful classical hardness, and learns efficiently under realistic noise — all at once.
status: Barren plateaus are established for important random-circuit regimes (McClean et al. (2018), *Barren Plateaus in Quantum Neural Network Training Landscapes*, arXiv:1803.11173; Huang et al. (2021), arXiv:2011.01938), but avoiding one obstruction alone does not establish the full conjunction.
solved_when: A single quantum-model family is exhibited that satisfies the full conjunction: it avoids barren plateaus, retains meaningful classical hardness, and learns efficiently under realistic noise.
why: It would reconcile the properties needed for a useful variational quantum learner, bridging the gap between circuits that train and circuits that matter.
key_works: McClean et al. (2018), *Barren Plateaus in Quantum Neural Network Training Landscapes*, arXiv:1803.11173; Huang et al. (2021), arXiv:2011.01938.

title: Beyond low-degree quantum-learning hardness
open: Are quantum state-learning and error-mitigation tasks that currently evade efficient estimators genuinely computationally hard, or do the known barriers merely reflect the limits of low-degree methods? The goal is to extend low-degree information–computation gaps to broader, model-independent computational hardness statements for specific state-learning and error-mitigation tasks.
status: A 2026 framework — Chen, Gong, Haferkamp, and Quek (2026), *Information-Computation Gaps in Quantum Learning via Low-Degree Likelihood* — establishes new low-degree information–computation gaps, including adaptive measurement settings; these remain model-specific lower bounds.
solved_when: A computational hardness statement is established for specific state-learning or error-mitigation tasks that goes beyond low-degree, model-specific lower bounds, e.g. by lifting the existing low-degree gaps (including those for adaptive measurement settings) to computational hardness under standard average-case hardness assumptions.
why: It would determine whether currently hard quantum inference tasks are fundamentally hard or merely defeat known estimators.
key_works: Chen, Gong, Haferkamp, and Quek (2026), *Information-Computation Gaps in Quantum Learning via Low-Degree Likelihood*.

title: Efficiently implementing instance-optimal quantum measurements
open: Can we turn an information-theoretic prescription for measuring a quantum system into something a lab can actually run — computing and physically implementing a near-optimal measurement design for a given observable family without the optimization or circuit cost eating up the sample savings it was supposed to deliver?
status: This is currently a research target. It is known that an information-theoretic formula involving Fisher information does not automatically provide efficient measurement synthesis. Related work includes Chen, Gong, and Zhou (2026), *Instance-Optimal High-Precision Shadow Tomography*; and Huang, Kueng, and Preskill (2020), *Predicting Many Properties of a Quantum System from Very Few Measurements*, arXiv:2002.08953.
solved_when: A procedure exists that, for a given family of observables, computes a measurement design achieving near-optimal sample complexity while its synthesis and implementation cost does not overwhelm the sample savings; no quantitative round counts or budgets are specified, so near-optimality plus implementation efficiency is the natural criterion.
why: It would convert sample-optimal quantum-learning theory into experimentally usable protocols.
key_works: Chen, Gong, and Zhou (2026), *Instance-Optimal High-Precision Shadow Tomography*; Huang, Kueng, and Preskill (2020), *Predicting Many Properties of a Quantum System from Very Few Measurements*, arXiv:2002.08953.

title: Generalization-theory falsification corpus
open: Can we build a controlled corpus of matched training runs that puts generalization theories to discriminating, falsifying tests? Specifically, a benchmark that systematically varies labels, parameterization, optimization, and data structure while holding competing complexity measures constant where possible.
status: Currently a proposed dataset target. Existing counterexamples and empirical studies provide components, not the complete controlled corpus specified here. Key works: Zhang et al. (2017), arXiv:1611.03530; Nagarajan and Kolter (2019), arXiv:1902.04742.
solved_when: A benchmark dataset exists containing matched training runs that systematically vary labels, parameterization, optimization, and data structure, with competing complexity measures held constant where possible.
why: It would let generalization theories make discriminating predictions instead of merely correlating with a small set of successful runs.
key_works: Zhang et al. (2017), arXiv:1611.03530; Nagarajan and Kolter (2019), arXiv:1902.04742.

title: Joint neural scaling phase-diagram measurements
open: What does neural network training behavior look like when we intervene jointly on width, depth, sample size, batch size, and learning rate, rather than one knob at a time? The goal is a preregistered grid measurement of training over these factors, with replicated seeds and complete trajectories recorded.
status: Currently a proposed dataset target only. Existing separate width-limit analyses and scaling-law fits do not substitute for the joint intervention grid. Key works: Yang et al. (2022), *Tensor Programs V*, arXiv:2203.03466; Cohen et al. (2021), *Edge of Stability*, arXiv:2103.00065.
solved_when: A preregistered factorial grid spanning width, depth, sample size, batch size, and learning rate is measured, with multiple seeds per cell and full training trajectories logged, and the dataset is released.
why: Joint measurements would expose interactions between scaling factors that one-variable-at-a-time scaling studies structurally cannot see, and would give the field a shared empirical substrate for testing scaling and training-dynamics theory.
key_works: Yang et al. (2022), *Tensor Programs V*, arXiv:2203.03466; Cohen et al. (2021), *Edge of Stability*, arXiv:2103.00065.

bib.title: Joint neural scaling phase-diagram measurements

title: Causal benchmark for in-context algorithm identification
open: Can we construct benchmark tasks for which different candidate learning algorithms implemented inside a model yield different predictions under carefully chosen prompt interventions, so that a model can be evaluated on which algorithm it actually implements rather than on ordinary task accuracy?
status: Proposed as a benchmark target building on linear-model and mechanistic studies of in-context learning, including Akyürek et al. (2023), *What Learning Algorithm Is In-Context Learning?*, arXiv:2211.15661, and Garg et al. (2022), arXiv:2208.01066; related work spans discriminating-input methods from system identification and mechanism interventions from causal inference.
solved_when: A benchmark suite exists in which prompt interventions distinguish candidate in-context learning algorithms by their predictions, and evaluation measures algorithm identification rather than standard accuracy.
why: Distinct internal algorithms can produce similar outputs on standard prompts, so ordinary accuracy does not reveal which learning algorithm a model implements in context.
key_works: Akyürek et al. (2023), *What Learning Algorithm Is In-Context Learning?*, arXiv:2211.15661; Garg et al. (2022), arXiv:2208.01066.

title: Federated participation and heterogeneity traces
open: Can the community obtain privacy-preserving datasets that record realistic client availability, local data distributions, drift, and communication constraints in federated settings? Formally, the target is traces with enough ground truth on participation and heterogeneity to test selection-bias corrections.
status: This is currently a proposed data target; existing federated benchmarks do not automatically meet this joint specification. Kairouz et al. (2021), *Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning*, arXiv:1912.04977; McMahan et al. (2017), arXiv:1602.05629.
solved_when: A released dataset exists that jointly captures client availability, local distributions, drift, and communication constraints in privacy-preserving form, with ground truth sufficient to evaluate selection-bias corrections.
why: Simulated independent participation can hide the failures most relevant to actual deployments; such traces would let selection-bias corrections be tested against realistic conditions rather than idealized ones.

title: End-to-end energy measurements for learning claims
open: Can the field agree on an end-to-end energy accounting protocol that makes learning-efficiency claims comparable across algorithms? Such a protocol would count data preparation, tuning, failed runs, training, inference, and verification when comparing algorithms at matched statistical quality.
status: Proposed as a measurement target only; no standardized protocol exists. Related fields include industrial ecology (lifecycle assessment) and computer architecture (energy accounting). Key works: Hoffmann et al. (2022), arXiv:2203.15556; Yang et al. (2022), *Tensor Programs V*, arXiv:2203.03466.
solved_when: A standardized measurement exists that counts data preparation, tuning, failed runs, training, inference, and verification at matched statistical quality, and efficiency claims (e.g., "10× cheaper," "100× more efficient") can be compared under it.
why: It would make "10× cheaper" or "100× more efficient" claims scientifically comparable; a reduction in nominal training operations is not automatically a reduction in total energy.
key_works: Hoffmann et al. (2022), arXiv:2203.15556; Yang et al. (2022), *Tensor Programs V*, arXiv:2203.03466.

title: Offline-decision benchmarks with hidden oracle separation
open: Can we build sequential-decision benchmarks that keep realistic logged data for the learner while holding counterfactual evaluation information separately aside, with auditably no leakage of oracle information into the learning pipeline?
status: Proposed benchmark target only. The known hazard is that a simulator's full state or reward oracle can silently give a learner stronger access than an offline theorem permits. Key works: Levine et al. (2020), *Offline Reinforcement Learning*, arXiv:2005.01643; Tkachuk et al. (2026), *Trajectory Data Suffices…*.
solved_when: A benchmark exists in which offline logged data is preserved for training, evaluation-only counterfactual information is maintained in isolation, and an audit mechanism demonstrably prevents oracle leakage.
why: It would make comparisons between offline-RL theory and experiments valid, closing the gap where a simulator's full state or reward oracle silently grants a learner stronger access than an offline theorem permits.
key_works: Levine et al. (2020), *Offline Reinforcement Learning*, arXiv:2005.01643; Tkachuk et al. (2026), *Trajectory Data Suffices…*.

title: Executable assumption contracts for learning algorithms
open: Can learning algorithms be shipped with executable "assumption contracts" — machine-readable statements of the conditions a theorem needs, paired with testable checks wherever such checks exist and explicit declarations where they do not? A complete answer is a standard packaging format under which any published learning algorithm carries its assumptions in a form both machines and humans can inspect.
status: This is a proposed infrastructure target, grounded in emerging testable-learning results; the key reference is Goel et al. (2026), *Testing Noise Assumptions of Learning Algorithms*, with related work in programming languages (contracts and refinement types) and formal verification (assume–guarantee reasoning).
solved_when: A specification and reference implementation exist in which algorithms are packaged with machine-readable assumptions, runnable tests for the checkable ones, and explicit declarations for those unverifiable from available data, such that hidden changes in noise, access model, distribution, or computational budget are surfaced before any theorem is invoked.
why: Today an algorithm's guarantees silently fail when the environment drifts from its assumed noise, access, distribution, or budget conditions; contracts would expose those violations mechanically instead of after a misleading deployment.
key_works: Goel et al. (2026), *Testing Noise Assumptions of Learning Algorithms*.

title: Hundredfold energy reduction with a matched statistical guarantee
open: For a clearly specified learning family, can we achieve a \(100\times\) reduction in measured lifecycle energy while preserving the same risk target, confidence level, and deployment workload? The challenge is to make this an algorithmic efficiency gain rather than a hardware or accounting substitution, by identifying the exploitable structure in the problem and counting all displaced costs.

(2022), *Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models*, arXiv:2203.15556 and McMahan et al. (2017), arXiv:1602.05629; connected themes include information-based complexity (energy-aware computation) and the thermodynamics of computation (physical resource limits).
solved_when: A clearly specified learning family exhibits \(100\times\) lower measured lifecycle energy at the same risk target, confidence level, and deployment workload, with the analysis of exploitable structure and all displaced costs made explicit.
why: It would establish a real algorithmic efficiency breakthrough rather than a hardware or accounting substitution.
key_works: Hoffmann et al. (2022), *Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models*, arXiv:2203.15556; McMahan et al. (2017), arXiv:1602.05629.

title: Independent longitudinal compute for theory-discriminating experiments
open: Can the field secure durable funding and compute access for longitudinal, preregistered training experiments that adjudicate between competing theories across multiple scales — including the publication of unsuccessful runs?

title: Funded maintenance of negative results and benchmark validity
open: How can we build a durable funding and governance mechanism that keeps theorem-status registries, replication artifacts, counterexamples, and benchmark contamination records maintained long after their original publication?

title: Fairness frontiers with selectively observed outcomes
open: What fairness–accuracy frontiers are achievable when the outcomes we wish to predict are only observed for individuals previously selected by earlier policies, and how much exploration is required to identify that frontier? Formally, characterize the joint set of achievable fairness and utility guarantees under selective-label feedback, including the minimum exploration budget needed.
status: Research target. Static postprocessing guarantees with fully observed outcomes do not resolve selective-label feedback; key works include Hardt, Price, and Srebro (2016), *Equality of Opportunity in Supervised Learning*, arXiv:1610.02413, and Liu et al. (2018), *Delayed Impact of Fair Machine Learning*, arXiv:1803.04383.
solved_when: A characterization exists of the achievable fairness–utility frontier under selective observation of outcomes, together with an identification of the minimum exploration needed to learn that frontier.
why: Historical decisions determine which outcomes become available for learning, so purely observational data may misstate the frontier unless exploration is accounted for.
key_works: Hardt, Price, and Srebro (2016), *Equality of Opportunity in Supervised Learning*, arXiv:1610.02413; Liu et al. (2018), *Delayed Impact of Fair Machine Learning*, arXiv:1803.04383.

title: Long-run welfare guarantees for adaptive fair policies
open: Can a learner acquire policies that honor explicitly specified long-run welfare constraints in settings where its own decisions reshape future group distributions and the transition dynamics must be learned rather than known in advance?
status: One-step delayed-impact models already show that static fairness criteria can harm intended beneficiaries (Liu, Dean, Rolf, Simchowitz, and Hardt (2018), *Delayed Impact of Fair Machine Learning*, arXiv:1803.04383; Perdomo et al. (2020), arXiv:2002.06673). Multi-step learning with welfare guarantees remains a stronger, unattained target.
solved_when: A learning procedure exists that, under an unknown transition model, provably satisfies the chosen long-run welfare constraints for policies whose decisions alter future group distributions.
why: Short-run parity is not a substitute for understanding long-run effects, so without such guarantees, fair-seeming policies may systematically harm the very groups they aim to protect.
key_works: Liu, Dean, Rolf, Simchowitz, and Hardt (2018), *Delayed Impact of Fair Machine Learning*, arXiv:1803.04383; Perdomo et al. (2020), arXiv:2002.06673.

title: Finite-sample validity of singular-model information criteria
open: Can we make information-criterion model comparison trustworthy at the finite sample sizes where it is actually used, when the models themselves are singular and grow with the data? Concretely, this asks for explicit finite-sample error bounds for WAIC- or WBIC-style comparisons in which model dimension and architecture complexity grow with sample size.
status: Asymptotic equivalences and singular-model criteria are established — Watanabe (2010), *Asymptotic Equivalence of Bayes Cross Validation and Widely Applicable Information Criterion in Singular Learning Theory*, and Watanabe (2013), *A Widely Applicable Bayesian Information Criterion* — but uniform finite-sample accuracy in growing deep models remains a separate target.
solved_when: Explicit finite-sample error bounds are derived for WAIC- or WBIC-style model comparisons, valid uniformly as model dimension and architecture complexity grow with sample size.
why: Practical model selection happens at finite sample sizes, often far from fixed-model asymptotics; without such bounds the criteria's guarantees do not apply to growing deep models.
key_works: Watanabe (2010), *Asymptotic Equivalence of Bayes Cross Validation and Widely Applicable Information Criterion in Singular Learning Theory*; Watanabe (2013), *A Widely Applicable Bayesian Information Criterion*.

title: Calibrated uncertainty on singular predictor quotients
open: Can we construct credible regions for identifiable predictive quantities whose uncertainty interpretation remains valid even when the model's parameter symmetries make the posterior geometry singular?
status: This is currently a research target; no construction is known. Parameter-space Gaussian approximations can be inappropriate when many parameters represent the same predictor. Key works: Watanabe (2013), *A Widely Applicable Bayesian Information Criterion*; Tinati and Tu (2026), *On the Asymptotics of Self-Supervised Pre-training*.
solved_when: A construction is given of credible regions for identifiable predictive quantities that retain valid uncertainty interpretation despite parameter symmetries and singular posterior geometry, where parameter-space Gaussian approximations fail.
why: It would make Bayesian uncertainty meaningful in overparameterized models without pretending their parameters are identifiable — the regime where Gaussian approximations in parameter space are inappropriate because many parameters represent the same predictor.
key_works: Watanabe (2013), *A Widely Applicable Bayesian Information Criterion*; Tinati and Tu (2026), *On the Asymptotics of Self-Supervised Pre-training*.

title: Singular learning theory with dependent and augmented samples
open: How do the learning coefficients and predictive-risk expansions of singular learning theory change when the observations are not independent — specifically, when they are dependent or produced by augmenting a smaller underlying sample? A formal answer would extend the singular asymptotic framework beyond the i.i.d. setting to these correlated-data regimes.
status: This is currently a research target; no resolution is recorded. The known pitfall is that treating augmented observations as independent can misstate the effective information available to a singular model. Relevant background includes Watanabe (2010), *Asymptotic Equivalence of Bayes Cross Validation and Widely Applicable Information Criterion in Singular Learning Theory*, and Holzman, Moran, and Shlimovich (2026), *Uniform Laws of Large Numbers in Product Spaces*, arXiv:2603.24493.
solved_when: A theory is available that determines the learning coefficients and predictive-risk expansions for singular models trained on dependent or augmented samples, replacing the assumption that augmented observations are independent with a correct account of the effective information they carry.
why: It would connect singular asymptotics to modern pretraining and augmentation workflows, where treating augmented observations as independent can misstate the effective information available to a singular model.
key_works: Watanabe (2010), *Asymptotic Equivalence of Bayes Cross Validation and Widely Applicable Information Criterion in Singular Learning Theory*; Holzman, Moran, and Shlimovich (2026), *Uniform Laws of Large Numbers in Product Spaces*, arXiv:2603.24493.
